Historia de los CDC Inglés (English) Imprimir Páginas relacionadas El 1 de julio de 1946 se abrió el Centro de Enfermedades Contagiosas ( Communicable Disease Center , CDC) en un piso de un pequeño edificio en Atlanta. Su misión principal era simple, aunque sumamente exigente: prevenir que el paludismo (malaria) se propagara por todo el país. Contando con un presupuesto de solo 10 millones de dólares y menos de 400 empleados, los primeros retos de la agencia incluyeron obtener suficientes camiones, rociadores y palas necesarios para desatar la guerra contra los mosquitos. Como la organización echó raíces en el sur, conocido alguna vez como el corazón de la zona del paludismo (malaria), el fundador de los CDC, el Dr. Joseph Mountin, continuó abogando por los problemas de salud pública y presionando a los CDC para que extendieran sus responsabilidades a otras enfermedades contagiosas. En 1947, los CDC hicieron un pago simbólico de $10 a la Universidad de Emory por 15 acres de tierra en Clifton Road en Atlanta donde ahora funciona la sede principal de los CDC. Hoy, los CDC son uno de los componentes principales de operación del Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos, y se reconocen como la agencia principal del país para la promoción de la salud, la prevención y la preparación. Presente y futuro Los CDC celebraron su sexagésimo aniversario en 2006. Hoy en día, los CDC son la primera agencia de promoción de la salud, prevención y preparación del país y una agencia líder mundial en el área de la salud pública. La agencia sigue a la vanguardia de los esfuerzos de salud pública destinados a prevenir y controlar las enfermedades crónicas e infecciosas, las lesiones, los riesgos ocupacionales, las discapacidades y las amenazas para la salud. Los CDC son reconocidos en todo el mundo por sus estudios y trabajos de investigación así como por ser una agencia orientada a la acción. Los CDC realizan actividades de investigación y aplican los resultados de esos estudios para mejorar la vida diaria de las personas y responder a las emergencias de salud; esta es una característica que los diferencia de otras agencias similares. Los CDC trabajan con los estados y otros socios para ofrecer un sistema de vigilancia de salud con el fin de monitorizar y prevenir brotes de enfermedades (incluso las relacionadas con el terrorismo biológico), implementar estrategias de prevención de enfermedades y mantener estadísticas nacionales de salud. Los CDC también realizan esfuerzos a nivel internacional contra la transmisión de enfermedades, para lo cual cuentan con personal en más de 25 países. La atención de los CDC se concentra actualmente en el logro de las cuatro metas fundamentales para la protección de la salud, con el fin de convertirse en una agencia de resultados concretos cuyo énfasis especial sea la gente sana, los lugares saludables, la preparación y la salud global. Los CDC son uno de los 13 componentes principales del Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos (HHS). pages.title: Innovation Takes Flight | National Geographic
pages.description: Global flight is changing. Discover how Honeywell Aerospace is developing technology that keeps pilots and passengers safe and connected.
pages.text: Innovation Takes Flight | National Geographic Paid Content for Honeywell Aerospace SCIENCE Innovation Takes Flight Global flight is changing. Discover how Honeywell Aerospace is developing technology that keeps pilots and passengers safe and connected. 11:38 When connectivity, autonomy, and safety systems just work, journeys feel seamless for passengers. Video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated November 11, 2026 Every flight begins with a simple expectation: to get from A to B safely. However, while air travel often feels simple and straightforward for passengers, every journey relies on a complex network of people, data, and technology working together to make it possible. As aviation evolves, this complexity does too. More passengers are taking to the skies, new technologies are entering the cockpit, and pilots have more data at their fingertips than ever before. The challenge is making sense of it all—harnessing the right information to make the right decisions at the right time. Not too long ago, pilots would begin their day by reading pages of flight information. Today, digital displays bring this information together, improving what pilots call situational awareness: their ability to build a clearer picture of what’s happening around them. All of which, “helps us make quicker, better decisions,” Jason Coffman, Commercial Airline Captain explains. Training has evolved too. Modern flight simulators can recreate the experience of flying an aircraft in remarkable detail, right down to turbulence in the air and bumps on the tarmac. This allows pilots to experience different scenarios in a controlled environment, preparing them for situations they may eventually encounter in real life. Honeywell Aerospace is helping shape how pilots interact with increasingly sophisticated aircraft systems. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions It is all part of the relationship between pilots and technology that has been evolving almost as long as aviation itself. Honeywell Aerospace has played a role in this story for more than a century, with innovations ranging from early autopilot technology to cabin pressure control systems. Today, the company is exploring an important question: as more technology enters the cockpit, how can it help pilots operate more safely without simply giving them more information to process? Distinguished Technical Fellow Thea Feyereisen specializes in human factors: how perception and cognition influence our interactions with technology. Throughout her time at Honeywell Aerospace, she has worked extensively on the science of cockpit alerts. With pilots processing multiple sources of information at once, how and when a new alert appears really matters. Because the right information at the right moment can change what happens next. In Thea’s words, it’s a balancing act between getting the pilots’ attention, but not “freaking them out so they don’t know how to respond.” Thea Feyereisen’s research focuses on translating systems innovation and human factors insights into engineered safety outcomes. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions A behind-the-scenes look at Honeywell Aerospace’s Surface Alert (SURF-A) system. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions In aviation technology, getting the balance right is critical—and Honeywell Aerospace’s Surface Alert (SURF-A) system illustrates this need perfectly. By monitoring the converging trajectories of aircraft, SURF-A can alert pilots up to 30 seconds before a potential runway collision occurs. The aim isn’t to make decisions on behalf of pilots, but to give them the precious time they need to recognize hazards and take corrective action. This principle extends beyond alerts. As automation plays a greater role in the cockpit, the relationship between pilot and technology becomes a balancing act of its own. How to Cite This Source As part of the U.S. government, information on EPA pages is a reliable and authoritative source for research. EPA.gov webpages do not have one author, so use “U.S. EPA” or “U.S. Environmental Protection Agency” in your sources. Find the last updated date at the bottom right of all EPA webpages. APA style Title of specific document. (Last update or copyright date; if not known, put n.d.). In title of website. Retrieved date, from link Example: What is Acid Rain? (2024). In EPA.gov. Retrieved May 7, 2024, from https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain Find more information about APA citations . Chicago Manual of Style "Title of specific page." Source. Last modified use the last modified date provided near the bottom of every page in month day, year format. Link. Example: "What is Acid Rain?" EPA.gov. Last modified May 7, 2024. https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain . Learn more information about Chicago style citations. MLA style "Title of specific page." USA.gov, use the last modified date provided near the bottom of every page in day abbreviated month. year format, link. Example: "What is Acid Rain?" EPA.gov, 7 May 2024, https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain . See more about creating an MLA citation . Principales capacidades Inglés (English) Imprimir Páginas relacionadas Promover la ciencia y la equidad en salud Plan estratégico de los CDC 2022-2027 Fuerza laboral de salud pública diversa Una fuerza laboral de salud pública diversa * garantiza que tengamos la capacidad para abordar enfermedades complejas y responder rápidamente a nuevas amenazas. Para lograr nuestra visión, los CDC tienen que formar y mantener una fuerza laboral científica y programática muy capacitada, a la vanguardia y flexible, que refleje a las comunidades en las que presta servicios, y apoyar el desarrollo de esa fuerza laboral a cada nivel del Gobierno en los Estados Unidos. Una fuerza laboral diversa y multidisciplinaria creará ambientes, políticas y prácticas más inclusivos y accesibles para tener un impacto más amplio en la salud pública. Datos y análisis de primera clase Desarrollar y usar datos y análisis de primera clase * , para fomentar la notificación continua de datos de laboratorio clínico y otros datos esenciales para la salud pública; garantizar la interoperabilidad entre los principales sistemas de vigilancia de salud pública; permitir el intercambio de datos seguro y bidireccional; y apoyar actualizaciones transversales, análisis avanzados y servicios compartidos. Como un recurso estratégico, los sistemas de datos de salud pública y los datos que los CDC recopilan deben estar conectados, y ser resilientes, adaptables y sostenibles. Estos sistemas y recursos deben administrarse e incorporar actualizaciones, integración y uso continuos. A través de monitoreo, modelización y análisis de brotes en tiempo real, los CDC convierten los datos en medidas de salud pública y prestan apoyo a los encargados de la toma de decisiones que necesitan información para mitigar los efectos de las amenazas de enfermedades, como los problemas sociales y económicos. Laboratorios de vanguardia Como el laboratorio de referencia para el mundo, los CDC deben garantizar que sus laboratorios estén a la vanguardia en ciencia, calidad y seguridad. Los CDC son un líder mundial en ciencias de laboratorio * , que es una parte esencial para el trabajo de los CDC. Los CDC, al colaborar con laboratorios de salud pública, deben tener suficiente competencia y capacidad para guiar las medidas de salud pública con amplia y confiable información científica. Respuesta rápida a los brotes en su origen Responder rápidamente a los brotes en su origen, tanto dentro del país como fuera de él. La principal responsabilidad de los CDC es responder a los brotes, los cuales son cada vez más complejos y frecuentes, para proteger la salud y el sustento, y salvar vidas. El mundo cuenta con los CDC para implementar intervenciones tempranas y estrategias de prevención adecuadas, equitativas e inmediatas, para evitar que algún brote agresivo se convierta en una epidemia y evitar que una epidemia en un país o una región se vuelva una pandemia mundial. Capacidad global y preparación nacional sólidas Construir sobre la base actual para lograr una capacidad de salud global y preparación nacional sólidas. La pericia estatal, local y comunitaria, y una presencia global estratégica reorientada a las regiones del mundo con el riesgo más alto ayudará a garantizar un sistema adaptable, resiliente y mejor coordinado, y países mejor preparados que puedan abordar las amenazas de las enfermedades en su origen. * Los enlaces a sitios web pueden llevar a páginas en inglés o español. pages.title: From Farm to Future | National Geographic
pages.description: Two farming families, thousands of miles apart, show how long-term resilience and strong relationships help them plan for what comes next.
pages.text: From Farm to Future | National Geographic Paid Content for Cargill ENVIRONMENT From Farm to Future Two farming families, thousands of miles apart, show how long-term resilience and strong relationships help them plan for what comes next. 14:24 Behind every meal are farmers, families, and a network of connections helping to keep food on our tables. Video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated November 13, 2026 Every meal begins long before we sit down to eat. Somewhere, a farmer is deciding what to grow, what to raise, and how to prepare for a future they can never fully predict. Months—sometimes years—before food reaches our plates, choices are being made that will help shape the meals we eat tomorrow. Those choices aren’t simple. Farmers invest before they know what prices they'll receive. They make plans before they know what the weather will bring. And they care for land they hope will support not only the next harvest, but the next generation. For most of us, this interconnected network of decisions remains largely out of sight. We walk into a grocery store and expect to find the shelves stocked, rarely pausing to think about the people, land, and relationships that make it all possible. Across the world, more than 600 million farmers are producing food for a global population of over eight billion. Their operations may look different, but they share a common responsibility: growing, raising, and producing the food people rely on every day. Cargill connects farmers’ harvests to the customers and markets that depend on them. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions In Colorado, father-and-son team Bob and Grant Bledsoe manage Bledsoe Cattle Company, a family operation that has been raising cattle in the American West for more than a century. Today, they oversee the family's ranch, farm, and feedlot, where their days rarely fit into the typical nine-to-five. More than 5,000 miles away in Poland, farming is also a family affair. Zygmunt and Paweł Wójtowicz grow grains, rapeseed, and corn across more than 2,700 acres. Zygmunt has worked the land for more than four decades, with Paweł helping to carry the business forward. The farms could hardly look more different. Different landscapes, different markets, different histories. Yet both families share a deep responsibility to the land and their livelihoods, while navigating forces beyond their control. “You can't fight Mother Nature,” shrugs Bob. “Most of the time, she smiles on us. And sometimes she doesn't.” Nature is only part of the uncertainty. Prices swing. Markets shift. Transportation can be disrupted. And the decisions farmers make today can shape their operations for seasons, sometimes generations, to come. Resilience matters. So do relationships. Cargill connects farmers’ harvests to the customers and markets that depend on them. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions No farm operates alone. Around it is a network of family, neighbors, communities, and partners helping farmers navigate uncertainty and plan for the future. For more than 160 years, Cargill has been an integral part of this network, working alongside farmers and helping connect what they produce to markets around the world. What that partnership looks like varies from farm to farm. Market insights can help inform decisions about what to produce, while risk-management tools provide more options around when and how to sell. As Cargill CEO Brian Sikes explains, support is always “unique to the individual farmer,” because “they know their land. They know their animals far better than we could ever know. So it’s our responsibility to sit with them, listen and understand the challenges and opportunities they’re facing on their individual farms.” For the Bledsoes, the relationship stretches back more than 35 years and has evolved beyond transactions into a longstanding partnership built on trust. pages.description: I Didn't Know That!: Leave No Trace Principle #6 - Respect Wildlife
pages.text: I Didn't Know That!: Leave No Trace Principle #6 - Respect Wildlife (U.S. National Park Service) Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us You’re visiting a park and notice a bison walk up a little way away from you. You’ve heard us joke about not petting the fluffy cows, but they just look so tame. Getting just a little closer to take an epic selfie won’t hurt... will it? There's not always a perfectly placed sign, so it's up to you to remember to keep your distance. NPS / Jacob W. Frank You aren’t visiting a zoo, you’re visiting a national park, a place to let wildlife be wild. The animals you see are not pets or cared for by staff, they are wild. Your safety, as well as the safety of the animals, depends on good judgement and following safe wildlife viewing guidelines. Did You Know? Respect Wildlife is one of the 7 Leave No Trace Principles . These Principles empower you to leave nature as unchanged by your presence as possible. It’s a way of protecting the natural world and yourself and to preserve our outdoor spaces for the enjoyment of generations to come. Why do I need to keep my distance? It keeps you safe . Remember that wildlife in parks is wild and can be unpredictable when disturbed or surprised. Interacting with wildlife can cause injury or disease. It keeps wildlife safe . Keeping your distance is not just for your safety, but also the safety of wildlife. Getting too close to wildlife can cause unnecessary stress. Animals can get injured trying to escape away from people who get close, especially near roads. Also, both people and pets may have diseases that they can give to wildlife. It’s the law . It’s illegal to feed, touch, tease, frighten, or intentionally disturb wildlife (36 CFR § 2.2(a)(2) Wildlife Protection). Safe Wildlife Viewing Guidelines Follow these three ranger tips to safely watch wildlife when visiting a park. 1. Know Before You Go Every park is unique and has specific guidelines, including minimum wildlife viewing distances. Before you head out, take a few minutes to review the park’s rules. Many parks have the Superintendent’s Compendium (park rules) available online on the park website, usually under “Learn About the Park” under “Management” and “Laws and Policies.” If you can’t access this information online or if you have questions, stop by the visitor center and ask a ranger. A spotting scope or a zoom lens is a great way to get a closer look while keeping safety in the picture. NPS Photo 2. Give Animals Room Parks provide a unique opportunity to view the natural behavior of animals in the wild. The best way to stay safe when watching wildlife is to give animals room to move. In general, if an animal reacts to your presence, you are too close. If you’re close enough for a selfie, you’re definitely too close! Use binoculars or a zoom lens and move back if wildlife approach you. Let wildlife be wild and observe from a distance. How Close is too Close? Many parks require you to stay a minimum distance of 25 yards from most wildlife and 100 yards from predators like bears and wolves. But make sure you check with the park you’re visiting as these rules sometimes vary (for example, Olympic National Park requires a minimum distance of 50 yards). pages.text: USAGov's mission and history | USAGov Skip to main content USAGov's mission and history Learn about the USAGov program and the U.S. government's official website, USA.gov. USA.gov is the official website of the U.S. government. The interagency site is managed by USAGov, a program within the U.S. General Services Administration's Technology Transformation Services . The USA.gov website is legislatively mandated through Section 204 of the E-Government Act of 2002 [PDF, 316KB] . USAGov's mission The mission of the USAGov program is to make it easier for people to find and understand the government services and information they need—anytime, anywhere, any way they want. In addition to USA.gov, the USAGov program serves people through the USAGov Contact Center , answering questions in about government services by phone or web chat. USAGov history The USAGov program has existed under various names for over 50 years, dating back to the Federal Information Center call centers in the 1960s and the Consumer Information Center, distributing government consumer booklets from Pueblo, Colorado beginning in the early 1970s. Read a blog post about how USAGov has been helping people through decades of cultural and technological change. The history of the USA.gov website Many people and organizations had a hand in creating this comprehensive portal to government. USA.gov got its start when internet entrepreneur Eric Brewer offered to donate a powerful search engine to the U.S. government in 1999. That gift helped speed up the government's earlier work to create a government-wide portal. And in 2000, USA.gov went live under the name FirstGov.gov. The General Services Administration and 22 federal agencies funded the initiative in 2001 and 2002. Since 2002, USA.gov has received an annual appropriation from the U.S. Congress. First launched in October 2003 under the name FirstGov.gov en Español, USAGov's Spanish language website was later renamed as GobiernoUSA.gov and then USAGov en Español. Access to this government information is now centrally provided only through USA.gov. In January 2007, FirstGov.gov officially changed its name to USA.gov. Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us Risks to People from Wildlife Smart Wildlife Watching Protects People National parks offer unique settings to watch wildlife in their natural habitats. And these experiences can have real health benefits, too. The sunshine helps you meet your daily Vitamin D recommendation, and scientists have linked time in nature to boosts in mental clarity, immunity, and happiness. Wildlife experiences can also bring on a sense of harmony, connectedness, and appreciation for nature. For the most part, staying safe while watching wildlife is easy: simply leave the wildlife alone. However, sometimes you might accidentally get too close to them on a trail or see other visitors unaware of the dangers, so it’s important to know the risks of getting too close to wild animals. The 7 Ways to Safely Watch Wildlife can help you avoid these risks: Diseases Carried by Animals Sometimes wildlife can get sick with zoonotic diseases, or diseases can be shared between animals and humans. These diseases are caused by a variety of pathogens (e.g. bacteria, viruses, fungi) and may cause fatal infections in people. Examples of zoonotic diseases include: rabies , hantavirus and tularemia . People can become infected with zoonotic diseases from contact with animal waste (feces and urine), being bitten by wildlife, or being bitten by disease vectors (e.g. fleas, ticks) that also feed on the blood of wildlife. Never touch wildlife, alive or dead, and be sure to tell a ranger if you see any wildlife acting strangely, like a bat flying in the daytime, for example. Keeping a safe distance from wildlife will minimize all potential routes of disease transmission. Your pets can also get diseases from wildlife. And pets can give some diseases to wildlife. To keep your pets and wildlife safe, be sure to keep pets on a leash, keep their vaccinations up to date, and don’t leave their food and water unattended. Better yet, leave them at home since many parks don’t allow pets on trails. Learn more about diseases shared between people and wildlife on the NPS One Health website . Deer Mouse NPS Photo / John Good Physical Injury from Wildlife Wild animals are unpredictable. When we get too close to wildlife, they might feel threatened and act in self-defense, especially if they have young nearby. Also, during mating season, many male animals, particularly ungulates like elk or bison, become territorial and may see you as a threat. That’s why each park requires visitors to stay a certain distance away from animals, usually 25 yards from most wildlife and 100 yards from large wildlife like bears or wolves. (Always check with the park you’re visiting, some parks require a minimum distance of 50 yards.) Remember, it’s your responsibility to maintain that distance. If wildlife approaches you, then you need to move back. Wildlife can be dangerous for your pets. Some animals, like moose, may feel your pet is a predator and may try to trample them. Pets also look like prey to many species of wildlife, so they will act accordingly, giving chase and possibly killing your pet, even when on a leash. Injuries from wildlife are not a pleasant way to spend your vacation. Bison and elk can gore, butt, or toss visitors and their pets. Snakes can strike, and bears can maul. Smaller wildlife such as squirrels and fox can bite and may carry ticks or fleas or rabies that can make you or your pet sick. pages.title: Brewing Resilience | National Geographic
pages.description: Across the world, coffee is a daily ritual. Learn what it takes to protect that ritual – and how illycaffè supports quality in every cup.
pages.text: Brewing Resilience | National Geographic Paid Content for Illycaffè ENVIRONMENT Brewing Resilience Across the world, coffee is a daily ritual. Learn what it takes to protect that ritual – and how illycaffè supports quality in every cup. 12:54 A simple cup of coffee depends on a world of connected expertise. VIDEO BY NICELY DONE PRODUCTIONS By Sam Kent Last updated November 2, 2026 For billions of people across the globe, coffee is part of the rhythm of everyday life. The first cup of the morning. A moment shared with friends. A familiar ritual played out in homes, cafés, and workplaces. Yet behind every cup is something far more complex. Before coffee reaches consumers, it begins life as a crop shaped by the conditions in which it grows. Much of it is grown within the coffee belt itself—a band of land around the equator where conditions traditionally allow coffee plants to thrive. However, today, those conditions are coming under threat. Rising temperatures, changing rainfall levels, and extreme weather are disrupting coffee-growing conditions and creating a more favorable environment for pests and diseases. For an industry built around such a sensitive agricultural product, maintaining quality is an ever-evolving challenge. Cristina Scocchia, Chief Executive Officer of illycaffè, describes coffee as a “living agricultural product”, whose quality depends on a finely tuned balance of soil, climate, and agricultural expertise. “Quality doesn’t come for free,” she explains. “Quality doesn’t simply happen.” The question becomes, therefore: As growing conditions change, how can the industry protect the crop – and the quality people around the world have come to expect? Changing temperatures and rainfall patterns are creating new challenges for coffee farmers. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions The answer starts with soil. For agronomists like César Augusto Correa Candiano, protecting the future of coffee begins from the ground up. Working alongside growers, César analyzes soil, leaves, and yields to understand what coffee plants need, while increasingly looking to regenerative agriculture to strengthen the land itself. This might mean planting cover crops around coffee plants, minimizing the use of chemicals, and recycling nutrients naturally. The goal is healthier soil and more resilient plantations—something César believes is essential to preserving coffee-growing land for generations to come. But expertise doesn’t only travel in one direction. In Tanzania, illycaffè discovered that coffee growers have been using a certain type of deep-rooted grass to help prevent soil erosion and conserve water. A regenerative practice born from farming experience rather than scientific theory. For David Brussa, Chief Total Quality & Sustainability Officer at illycaffè, discoveries like this demonstrate the value of looking beyond the laboratory for answers. It’s an exchange of knowledge that really matters. Because, when you’re dealing with such a complex product, ensuring quality depends on learning from every stage of its journey. Coffee is a remarkably complex product, with hundreds of chemical compounds contributing to the flavors and aromas we experience. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions Close-up of roasted coffee beans piled together in warm, low light. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions “Like olive oil and wine, the taste [of coffee is] dependent on the type of soil,” David explains. From fertility and farming practices to the way the beans themselves are roasted, numerous variables can influence the final cup. And managing these variables has long been central to illycaffè’s approach. Coffee itself is remarkably complex—green coffee contains around 300 molecules, rising to around 1,200 after roasting. With so many variables at play, the challenge is maintaining consistent quality and taste, cup after cup. pages.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history' British Broadcasting Corporation British Broadcasting Corporation
pages.description: The Ukrainian president says the slowed-down internet is making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
pages.text: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history' Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history' 6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Dan Sales Reuters Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said. The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks. Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment. US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace. The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump. Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back". It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented. The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher. On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there". "Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design. On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine. "It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying. Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets. Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said. pages.description: Interstate Air Pollution Transport, also known as Air Transport, is when air pollution travels over distances, affecting air quality and public health locally and regionally.
pages.text: Cross-State Air Pollution | US EPA Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Cross-State Air Pollution The total pollution in any area forms from the combination of local and upwind sources. Air transport refers to pollution from upwind emission sources that impact air quality in a given location downwind. Emissions of sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) and nitrogen oxides (NO X ) can each undergo chemical reactions in the atmosphere to form fine particle (soot) pollution. Similarly, NO X emissions can react in the atmosphere to create ground-level ozone (smog) pollution. These pollutants can travel great distances affecting air quality and public health regionally. The transport of these pollutants across state borders, referred to as interstate air pollution transport, makes it difficult for downwind states to meet health-based air quality standards for PM 2.5 and ozone. The "Good Neighbor" Provision The Clean Air Act 's "good neighbor" provision requires EPA and states to address interstate transport of air pollution that affects downwind states' ability to attain and maintain National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) . Specifically, Clean Air Act section 110(a)(2)(D)(i)(I) requires each state in its State Implementation Plan (SIP) to prohibit emissions that will significantly contribute to nonattainment of a NAAQS, or interfere with maintenance of a NAAQS, in a downwind state. The Act requires EPA to backstop state actions by promulgating Federal Implementation Plans (FIPs) in the event that a state fails to submit or EPA disapproves good neighbor SIPs. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Public Input & Actions BLM Transitions to Winter Motor Vehicle Limitations for the White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area Alaska Fairbanks DO Eastern Interior FO Media Contact Deanna DePue Deanna_depue@ios.doi.gov BLM Office: Eastern Interior Field Office October 28, 2026 FAIRBANKS, Alaska – Effective immediately, the Bureau of Land Management is transitioning to winter motor vehicle limitations in the White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area. This change comes because the area now has adequate snow cover in place. This ends the temporary extension of summer motor vehicle limitations issued on October 14, 2026, which was done to allow time for snow accumulation to reduce trail and resource damage. Public access to both areas is permitted in accordance with applicable regulations and land use plans. During the winter season, the White Mountains are open to the use of snowmobiles weighing up to 1,000 pounds curb weight and up to 50 inches wide, in addition to all forms of non-motorized use. Winter trails are open to both snowmobiles and non-motorized users, except for the non-motorized Ski Loop Trail and Summit Trail. While many boundaries and trails are marked to help with navigation, some trail work is still in progress, and some areas may not be well marked. To assist with navigation and learn more about motor vehicle limitations, visitors are encouraged to use the BLM’s georeferenced PDF maps for Summer Recreation and Winter Recreation . More information is available on the BLM Georeferenced PDF Maps webpage, including tips for using georeferenced map applications and your mobile device’s GPS to navigate in areas without cellular service. When riding the trails, please travel responsibly, wear a helmet and ride to reduce damage to the surrounding area and resources. For access information and useful links, monitor the White Mountains Trail Updates . For more information contact the BLM Fairbanks Public Room at (907) 474-2200 or 1-800-437-7021. The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

pages.description: Smart Wildlife Watching Protects Animals
pages.text: Risks to Wildlife from People - Watching Wildlife (U.S. National Park Service) Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us Risks to Wildlife from People Smart Wildlife Watching Protects Wildlife Watching wildlife safely is the responsibility of all park visitors. When you visit national parks, you are entering animals’ habitat and should behave like a polite guest. In fact, the safety and health of wildlife depends on the thoughtful choices park visitors make. Wildlife face some serious risks when humans get close enough to interact with them: Bison resting in Yellowstone. NPS Photo / Neil Herbert Consequences of Physical Contact with People Although many wildlife appear tame, they are not. It is important to resist the urge to pet and hold them. In fact, some animals, from bison to birds, may be rejected by their parents if they have contact with humans, making them more vulnerable to predators or other harmful situations. In addition, wildlife can get injured when they try to escape people who have gotten too close, especially if they are near human structures or roads. Wildlife that get used to being around people and developed areas such as picnic areas and campgrounds also are at greater risk of eating human food and catching diseases from people and pets or giving diseases to humans and their pets. Visitors walk a dog on a leash in Arches National Park NPS / Veronica V. Fatal Diseases from People and Pets Our domestic pets can also pose real dangers to the wildlife within parks. Both pets and people may have diseases that they can give to wildlife. Sadly, there are many examples of wildlife in parks dying from diseases given to them by pets and humans. For example, heartworm from dogs and cats can kill wildlife such as foxes, wolves, coyotes, bobcats, and mountain lions. Black-footed ferrets die from the flu if humans are sick and get too close. Wolves can be infected by canine parvovirus from dogs and many animals can be affected by toxoplasmosis, which is carried by cats. Pro tip: Keeping your pets vaccinated can keep them and wildlife safe. Store food in bear boxes when provided. NPS Photo / Jacob W. Frank Dangers of Eating Human Food and/or Trash When visitors intentionally or unintentionally feed wildlife, it has negative effects on the wildlife. Whether visitors offer scraps and crumbs to birds and other wildlife or simply forget to secure their trash, risks to wildlife from eating human food are great. Some of the dangers to wildlife include shorter lives and poor nourishment. The best way for wildlife to have a healthy diet and live healthy lives is to hunt, forage, or scavenge for food as they would naturally. Relying on human food (which includes trash left out!) puts wildlife at risk. Human food can also boost some animal populations, which can then result in increased predation on threatened and endangered species like the marbled murrelet or piping plover. Learning to eat human food can also change the way that wildlife interact with people. The process of wild animals becoming used to and attracted to human food is called “food conditioning.” Food-conditioned animals actively seek out human food, which in the worst cases can make them dangerous. Ground squirrels can bite, deer have sharp hooves and antlers, and bears can rip into cars or tents in search of food. Unfortunately, food-conditioned wildlife that become too aggressive must be removed, which can include being humanely killed by park managers for safety reasons. Lenders must document the business reason and justification for their decisions and retain these and supporting documents, as outlined in SOP 50 57-2 , Chapter 6 and Chapter 8, in the loan file for future SBA review to determine if the actions taken were prudent, commercially reasonable (consistent with generally accepted commercial lending practices) and complied with applicable loan program requirements. pages.title: ‘Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?’: Republicans reckon with Arizona wipeout | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
pages.description: When Trump was first elected, Republicans held every lever in Arizona – now they’ve been swept in a blue tidal wave, and the road to rebuild could be fraught
pages.text: ‘Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?’: Republicans reckon with Arizona wipeout | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Republican supporters at an election night watch party in Scottsdale in 2018. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Republican supporters at an election night watch party in Scottsdale in 2018. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images US midterm elections 2026 ‘Were we too Maga or not Maga enough?’: Republicans reckon with Arizona wipeout When Trump was first elected, Republicans held every lever in Arizona – now they’ve been swept in a blue tidal wave, and the road to rebuild could be fraught Mary Jo Pitzl in Phoenix Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.03 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen Donald Trump was first elected to the White House in 2016, Republicans held every lever of statewide power in Arizona, from the governor’s office to both US Senate seats and majorities in the legislature. Over the next decade, as Trump tightened his grip on the party, Democrats began chipping away at that dominance, gradually turning the longtime GOP stronghold into a political battleground. Then came the November midterm elections. Democrats swept every statewide office on the ballot – from governor to the obscure post of mine inspector – and secured a lawmaking trifecta unseen since 1966. The results leave Republicans firmly locked out of power at the state level – a remarkable reversal of fortunes for the long-dominant party that was once home to Barry Goldwater’s rock-ribbed conservatism and John McCain’s maverick streak. “I could see this coming,” said Gina Swoboda, a former chair of the Arizona Republican party. “We weren’t talking to people, we weren’t listening to people.” Swoboda tried. This year, she ran for secretary of state, to serve as the state’s chief elections officer. She lost the Republican primary to Alexander Kolodin, a Trump acolyte who was heavily involved in efforts to overturn the 2020 election results in the state. Last Tuesday, Kolodin was trounced by the Democratic incumbent, Adrian Fontes. View image in fullscreen Gina Swoboda, a former GOP chair in Arizona, during a Trump rally in 2024. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Getty Images In several closely watched races, Trump allies fell. Congressman Andy Biggs, a longtime supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, lost by more than 10 percentage points to Katie Hobbs, the Democratic incumbent once viewed as vulnerable. So seismic were the gains that a 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University bested a tenured Republican to become the superior county clerk of Maricopa county – in charge of court records, marriage licenses, child support and other filings for the fourth largest county in America. The Republican collapse in Arizona were part of a blue tidal wave that swept GOP officials from power in even redder states, such as South Carolina and Texas. But in Arizona, a state reshaped by decades of demographic change, a population boom in the Phoenix suburbs and a rejection of Trumpism by affluent Republican and independent voters, the GOP now faces a reckoning that many say might have come eventually but now cannot be delayed. “The world has changed, so if there is no change from the party, we’ll be looking at minority status for a long time,” said Kirk Adams, a former Arizona house speaker who served as chief of staff to the last Republican governor. “Political parties tend to react to near-extinction events like this.” Among the most urgent questions facing Republicans in the Grand Canyon state is how to rebuild. Republicans hold a nearly 300,000 voter-registration advantage over Democrats in the state, but independent voters make up the largest share of the electorate, and often decide elections. Sections: Progress Report Home | Program Basics | Emissions Reductions | Emission Controls & Monitoring | Program Compliance & Market Activity | Air Quality | Atmospheric Deposition | Ecosystem Response Power Sector Programs - Progress Report Progress Report Story Map Learn about EPA's power sector programs and their progress in this interactive story map . The Power Sector Programs Progress Report provides annual updates on EPA’s regulatory programs to reduce emissions in the power sector. Click one of the sections below to get started. Progress Report Fact Sheet (pdf) (3.02 MB, October, 2024) See the index of graphics in this report . Under the Clean Air Act, EPA implements regulations to reduce emissions from power plants, including the Acid Rain Program (ARP), the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR), the CSAPR Update, the Revised CSAPR Update, and the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS). These programs require fossil fuel-fired electric generating units to reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ), nitrogen oxides (NO X ), and hazardous air pollutants including mercury (Hg) to protect human health and the environment. This reporting year marks the seventh year of CSAPR implementation, the fifth year of the CSAPR Update implementation, the first year of Revised CSAPR Update implementation, the twenty-seventh year of the ARP, and the fifth year of MATS implementation. This report summarizes annual progress, highlighting data that EPA systematically collects on emissions for all power plant programs and on compliance for the ARP and the CSAPR programs. Commitment to transparency and data availability is a hallmark of these programs and a cornerstone of their success. SO 2 , NO X , and hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), including mercury, are fossil fuel combustion byproducts that affect public health and the environment. SO 2 and NO X , and their sulfate and nitrate byproducts, are transported downwind and deposited as acid rain which can be harmful to sensitive ecosystems in many areas of the country. These pollutants also contribute to the formation of fine particles (sulfates and nitrates) and ground-level ozone that are associated with significant human health effects and regional haze. Atmospheric mercury deposition accumulates in fish to levels of concern for human health and the health of fish-eating wildlife. The ARP, CSAPR, CSAPR Update, Revised CSAPR Update, and MATS have delivered substantial reductions in power sector emissions of SO 2 , NO X , and hazardous air pollutants, along with significant improvements in air quality and the environment. In addition to the requirement of the power sector emission control programs described in this report, a variety of power industry trends have contributed to further declines of SO 2 , NO X , and hazardous air pollutant emissions. Oak Ridge Office of Environmental Management Mission Our mission is to complete the safe cleanup of environmental legacies on the Oak Ridge Reservation resulting from decades of nuclear weapons development and government-sponsored nuclear energy research. Our projects are protecting the region's health and environment by removing risks, enabling modernization at national security and science sites, and transferring cleaned land to the community to boost new economic growth. pages.text: Options for Returning Government Property July 16 – August 15, 2025 | FDA Skip to main content Skip to FDA Search Skip to in this section menu Skip to footer links Home About FDA Resources for Former FDA Employees Options for Returning Government Property July 16 – August 15, 2025 Resources for Former FDA Employees In this section Employees separated from the FDA must return Government property directly to FDA, including accountable property (laptops, tablets, phones, MiFis, IronKeys, etc.), non-accountable Government property (monitors, keyboards, chairs, etc.), and FDA Personal Identification Verification (PIV) cards/badges, FDA Credentials, and FDA Passports. Separated Employees Retrieving Personal Items: Contact your supervisor or call the Employee Resource and Information and Center (ERIC) at 301 827-3742 or 866-807-3742 to request an escort. You will be asked to provide your name, preferred contact information, the building you wish to access, and your Center/Office/Program. ERIC will forward your request to a coordinator who will assist with scheduling a date and time for your escort. Separated Employees Returning Government Property and PIV Cards/Badges and Credentials: Individuals Located Within 50 Miles of the White Oak Campus or 5630 Fishers Lane: Return items at the White Oak Building 62 loading dock or the lower-level, FDA entrance to 5630 Fishers Lane, Rockville, MD, on weekdays through Wednesday, August 15, 2025, from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Appointments are unnecessary. Individuals Located Within 50 Miles of a Field Location: Call the Employee Resource and Information and Center (ERIC) at 301-827-3742 or 866-807-3742 to request dates and times during which the facility can accept returns. Individuals Located More Than 50 Miles from an FDA Location: Call ERIC at 301-827-3742 or 866-807-3742 to request a mailing label and shipping instructions. Note: PIV cards must be defaced (e.g., hole-punched) before mailing. Separated Employees Who Need to Return FDA Passports: Email FDAPassportOffices@fda.hhs.gov to schedule an appointment with the Passport Office at White Oak or to request a mailing label and shipping instructions. Plan estratégico de los CDC, 2022-2027 Imprimir Páginas relacionadas Promover la ciencia y la equidad en salud Plan estratégico de los CDC, 2022-2027 El plan estratégico de los CDC para el periodo 2022-2027 fomenta la ciencia y la equidad en salud, y afirma el compromiso de la agencia con una visión unificada, la de proteger de forma equitativa la salud y la seguridad. El plan sigue potenciando 5 capacidades principales de la agencia, al reflejar nuestro compromiso con la equidad y la diversidad, y al impulsar las áreas en las que hemos invertido durante la pandemia de COVID-19. pages.text: Your Rights Under USERRA Poster | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Your Rights Under USERRA Poster Employers are required to provide to persons entitled to the rights and benefits under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), a notice of the rights, benefits and obligations of such persons and such employers under USERRA. Employers may provide the notice, “Your Rights Under USERRA”, by posting it where employee notices are customarily placed. However, employers are free to provide the notice to employees in other ways that will minimize costs while ensuring that the full text of the notice is provided (e.g., by handing or mailing out the notice, or distributing the notice via electronic mail). USERRA Poster (PDF) Sus Derechos Bajo USERRA – Póster Los empleadores están obligados a proporcionar a las personas con derechos y beneficios en virtud de la Ley de Derechos de Empleo y Reempleo de los Servicios Uniformados (USERRA), un aviso de los derechos, beneficios y obligaciones de dichas personas y de dichos empleadores en virtud de USERRA. Los empleadores pueden proporcionar el aviso, “Sus Derechos Bajo USERRA”, publicándolo donde los avisos de los empleados se colocan habitualmente. Sin embargo, los empleadores tienen la libertad de proporcionar el aviso a los empleados de otras maneras que minimicen los costos, siempre y cuando se garantice que se proporcione el texto completo del aviso (por ejemplo, entregando o enviando el aviso por correo, o distribuyendo el aviso por correo electrónico). BLM photo by Jim Herriges. FAIRBANKS, Alaska – The Bureau of Land Management Eastern Interior Field Office will open the winter Fortymile caribou federal subsistence hunt in Units 20E, 25C and a portion of 20F on October 27, 2026. This hunt is limited to federally qualified rural residents hunting on federal public lands only, including federal public lands accessible from the Steese, Elliott, and Taylor highways. The winter federal subsistence hunt opens at 12:01 a.m. on October 27, 2026, in all Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) State Fortymile Caribou Zones with a harvest limit of one bull caribou . If a federally qualified subsistence user has harvested a caribou in any other federal or State hunt since July 1, 2026, an additional caribou cannot be harvested during this winter federal subsistence hunt. The hunt closes at 11:59 p.m. on March 31, 2027, unless otherwise modified during the season, such as by emergency special action to prevent overharvest. The BLM may issue emergency special actions to delay opening dates or to close zones with short notice to prevent overharvest. Announcements notifying the public of any changes will be posted at least three days before the action would take effect. The public should closely monitor the Fortymile Caribou Hotline at (907) 267-2310 for updates. Federally qualified subsistence hunters must obtain a RC867 joint State/federal permit issued by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game . If the State hunt is closed, federally qualified hunters may only harvest on federal public lands. When the State portion of RC867 is open, federal hunters may hunt on federal lands and all open state lands. Hunters should review the RC867 permit conditions. The harvest limit of one caribou applies to the entire regulatory year and is not additive to other federal or state hunts. Evidence of external sex organs must remain attached and all reporting requirements apply. Federal subsistence hunting is not allowed on lands selected by Alaska Native Corporations, Native allottees, or the State of Alaska. Maps showing federal public lands open to the hunt near the Steese and Taylor highways are available from the BLM Alaska Public Rooms and in the “Federal Subsistence Hunting Map Series” in the BLM Alaska’s georeferenced PDF map collection. This collection also includes the “Digital Public Information Map Series,” featuring maps with information about BLM recreation sites and motor vehicle access; however, these maps include general land status and do not indicate closures due to land selections. Please see the BLM Alaska Travel and Transportation Plans for the White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area for information on BLM travel limitations. Updates on current conditions affecting travel in these areas, including the summer travel extension to November 1, 2026, are available on the BLM White Mountains National Recreation Area trail updates webpage . pages.text: Where Trump and Republicans lost the midterms – a visual analysis of the key states | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation US midterm elections 2026 Where Trump and Republicans lost the midterms – a visual analysis of the key states The Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives. These charts and maps reveal the key trends and races behind this result Live results from all 50 states Reader Q&A: What happens after the ‘blue wave’? Alex Clark , Andrew Witherspoon , Will Craft and Ashley Kirk Thu 5 Nov 2026 03.34 EST First published on Wed 4 Nov 2026 08.06 EST Share The Republicans have lost seven Senators, 30 House districts and five governor races. As of 3.30am Eastern Time (ET) on Thursday, more than 2,000 of nearly 2,500 counties with Senate elections had returned more than 90% of their votes. Americans did not turn out in significant numbers for the Republicans amid high fuel prices and dissatisfaction with the president. This allowed the Democrats to pick up a number of seats – and take back control of the US House of Representatives and Senate. Here’s how it happened. In the Senate the midterm results have given Democrats the ability to put a serious check on Trump's agenda – including blocking any new appointments to the supreme court or his cabinet. Republicans had previously held a majority of 53 seats out of 100 – but this has now been emphatically overturned. Thirty-five seats were on the ballot. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third facing voters at each two-year election cycle. In practice, the battle for the Senate was fought across a very small map. The Cook Political Report – a prominent US election forecaster – had listed six seats as tossups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Democrats have won most of the races viewed as competitive before the election Results versus Cook Political Report ratings of competitiveness pre-election Hold Flip Undeclared Forecast Result Likely Democrat Lean Democrat Toss-up Lean Republican Likely Republican 0 of 0 key races declared Cook Political Report ratings, as of 30 October 2026 Democrats had to flip at least four seats that were held by Republicans to gain a majority. They surpassed this target. In an early sign of the Democrats’ momentum, the party won the Senate race in Texas , a longstanding Republican stronghold. In the run-up to the election, polls had shown a razor-thin lead for the Democratic candidate. The actual result was, in fact, record-breaking – with James Talarico winning the seat by more than 10 points. No Democrat had won a Senate seat in Texas since 1988. pages.text: Seeking, Negotiating, and Post Employment Restrictions | FDA Skip to main content Skip to FDA Search Skip to in this section menu Skip to footer links Home About FDA Jobs at FDA Ethics Seeking, Negotiating, and Post Employment Restrictions Ethics In this section Seeking and Negotiating Future Non-Federal Employment What is the rule? What is the rationale for the ethics restrictions? What activities constitute “seeking employment”? What is the scope of the recusal requirement when I am seeking employment? What do I do when I become aware of the need to recuse myself from a particular matter? May I accept interview expenses? I am a procurement official; are there special rules? Are there other considerations to keep in mind? Are there additional resources about seeking or negotiating for non-federal employment? Post-Employment Restrictions Former employees are subject to the provisions described below. Former government attorneys and public officials with a law license are subject to additional post-employment restrictions under State Rules of Professional Conduct. Political appointees are subject to additional Ethics Pledge requirements under EO 13989 . Public financial disclosure filers must file an OGE Form 278e Termination report within 30 days after leaving HHS unless they enter into another public financial disclosure filing position within those 30 days. Certain exceptions, not discussed here, may apply in limited circumstances. Contact OEI at FDAEthics_Advice@fda.hhs.gov for further information. May I contact FDA on behalf of others? May I provide assistance to others? Are there additional restrictions for senior FDA employees? What is a “senior employee”? Are there other restrictions? Are there additional resources about leaving federal service? Rule In general, an executive branch employee is free to seek post-Government employment with any non-Government entity, but the employee may need to recuse from working on some Government matters while doing so. A criminal conflict of interest statute, 18 U.S.C. § 208, prohibits an employee from participating personally and substantially, in an official capacity, in any "particular matter" that, to the employee's knowledge, would have a direct and predictable effect on the employee's financial interests or on the financial interests of a person or organization with whom the employee is negotiating or has an arrangement concerning prospective employment. A related executive branch-wide regulation, Subpart F of 5 C.F.R. part 2635, prohibits an employee from working on a particular matter if the employee is "seeking employment" with a person or organization affected by that matter, even though the employee's job search has not progressed to actual negotiations. An employee who complies with the recusal requirements in Subpart F will ensure compliance with the conflict of interest statute. Back to Top Rationale An FDA employee’s experience and expertise may make the employee attractive to a non-Federal employer. If you are seeking post-FDA employment and your FDA work could benefit a potential employer, the public may be concerned that your work could inappropriately favor the prospective employer. Accordingly, you may be disqualified from working on particular FDA matters while seeking post-FDA employment. Back to Top How do I know? An employee is "seeking employment" as defined in Subpart F, and the recusal requirement applies, if: ​​​​​​​the employee is engaged in actual negotiations for employment; a prospective employer has contacted the employee about possible employment and the employee makes a response other than rejection; or the employee has contacted a prospective employer about possible employment, unless the sole purpose of the contact is to request a job application. (An employee is seeking employment with any person to whom he sends an unsolicited resume, regardless of how many resumes the employee sends to other employers at the same time.) pages.text: Monitoring Surface Water Chemistry | US EPA Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Monitoring Surface Water Chemistry Surface water chemistry is a direct indicator of the effects of acid rain on water bodies. Networks that monitor surface water chemistry over long time periods provide valuable information on aquatic ecosystem health and how water bodies respond to changes in acid-causing emissions. EPA oversees the Long-Term Monitoring (LTM) program, which tracks changes in surface water chemistry in response to changing air pollution and acid deposition. The goal of this long-term program is to track whether the Clean Air Act Amendments (CAAA) ( Plain English Guide to the Clean Air Act ) have been effective in reducing the acidity of surface waters in New England, the Northern Adirondack Mountains, Appalachian Plateau, and the Central Appalachians and advance the science of air pollution impacts on water resources. What are Acidified Surface Waters? Acid precipitation (commonly known as acid rain) primarily affects sensitive bodies of water, which are located in watersheds whose soils have a limited ability to neutralize acidic compounds (called “buffering capacity”). Acidification is a result of acidic deposition and the soil’s capacity to buffer what is deposited. As water moves through and over the soil, it picks up the acid deposited and transfers it into lakes and streams. As lakes and streams become more acidic, the numbers and types of fish and other aquatic plants and animals that live in these waters decrease. Locations for the LTM Program The LTM program tracks changes in surface water chemistry in the four regions shown below, known to be sensitive to acid rain: New England, the Adirondack Mountains, the Northern Appalachian Plateau, and the central Appalachians.   Open the map full screen. Data for the LTM Program Data Link: EPA Long-Term Monitoring of Acidified Surface Waters This dataset compiles surface water chemistry data for 172 sites (lakes and streams) from 1980 to 2018 and will be updated annually with an approximate lag time of one year. Data are currently collected from 158 sites in four regions sensitive to acid rain in the eastern United States: Central Appalachians (Virginia), Adirondack Mountains (New York), Catskills (New York), New England (Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont). The fifth region/state (Pennsylvania) is no longer sampled but is still included in the dataset. Fourteen sites in the four regions are no longer sampled, but are also included in the dataset. These data are used to calculate trends in surface water chemistry to assess aquatic ecosystem response to changes in sulfur and nitrogen deposition. Water chemistry in this data can be influenced by the ambient flow conditions, such as spring snowmelt or intense rainfall. To be included in the dataset, sites needed to have regular sampling (at least once per year for 20 years). Organización de los CDC Inglés (English) Imprimir Páginas relacionadas Los CDC son uno de los componentes operativos más importantes del Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos. Vea las declaraciones oficiales sobre la misión de los CDC y su organigrama (en inglés) para saber más acera de la estructura organizacional de los CDC. Misión de los CDC Los CDC trabajan a toda hora para proteger a los Estados Unidos contra amenazas a la salud y seguridad, provenientes del exterior o dentro del país. Independientemente de que las enfermedades se originen en los Estados Unidos o en otros países, sean crónicas o agudas, curables o prevenibles, sean el resultado de error humano o de un ataque intencional, los CDC luchan contra las enfermedades, y apoyan a las comunidades y a los ciudadanos para que hagan lo mismo. Los CDC aumentan la seguridad de la salud en nuestro país. Como la agencia de protección de la salud del país, los CDC salvan vidas y protegen a la gente de las amenazas a la salud. Para cumplir con nuestra misión, los CDC hacen investigaciones científicas vitales y proporcionan información de salud que protege a nuestro país de las peligrosas y costosas amenazas a la salud, y responden cuando estas surgen Más Organigrama de los CDC Organigrama de los CDC [PDF – 86 KB] Última revisión: el 24 de febrero del 2023 Fuente: Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Public Input & Actions BLM Extends Summer Motor Vehicle Limitations for the White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area Alaska Fairbanks DO Eastern Interior FO Media Contact Deanna DePue Deanna_depue@ios.doi.gov BLM Office: Eastern Interior Field Office October 14, 2026 FAIRBANKS, Alaska – Due to the lack of adequate snow cover, the Bureau of Land Management is extending summer motor vehicle limitations in the White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area until November 1, 2026. The summer extension allows continued use of wheeled off-highway vehicles (OHVs) under the summer weight limitations, while motorized vehicle use in winter motorized areas remains limited until adequate snow cover is present. Typically, the BLM transitions to winter motor vehicle restrictions in these areas on October 15. This year’s snow cover is not expected to reach the target depth of six inches prior to this summer-to-winter transition date. As a result, the Eastern Interior Field Office is extending the summer authorization for wheeled OHV use that would be otherwise prohibited under the winter limitations; winter motorized limitations authorize snowmobile only. The White Mountains National Recreation Area and Steese National Conservation Area remain open to all forms of non-motorized use year-round, including hiking, equestrian, and bicycling. Winter motor vehicle limitations will now be in effect Nov. 1 – April 30. If target snow cover depths are reached sooner, an earlier transition date will be announced. While many boundaries and trails are marked to help with navigation, some trail work is still in progress, and some areas may not be well marked. To assist with navigation and learn more about motor vehicle limitations, visitors are encouraged to use the BLM’s georeferenced PDF maps for Summer Recreation and Winter Recreation . More information is available on the BLM Georeferenced PDF Maps webpage , including tips for using georeferenced map applications and your mobile device’s GPS to navigate in areas without cellular service. When riding the trails, please travel responsibly, wear a helmet and ride to reduce damage to the surrounding area and resources. For access information and useful links, monitor the White Mountains Trail Update s . For more information, contact the BLM Fairbanks Public Room at (907) 474-2200. The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

pages.title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth | California | The Guardian
pages.description: Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars
pages.text: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth | California | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Supporters hold signs advocating for the Billionaire Tax Now coalition in Los Angeles in April. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Supporters hold signs advocating for the Billionaire Tax Now coalition in Los Angeles in April. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images California California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars Dara Kerr Mon 9 Nov 2026 21.54 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 15.53 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth. The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and Democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom , the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Donald Trump ’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”. The Associated Press called the race late Monday night with 83% of the votes in. Of that count, 52.8% of people voted no and 47.2% voted yes. “Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the no on Prop 40 campaign said in a statement. “It was built on false assumptions and promises, flawed in its design and execution, and reliant on economic theories rejected many times over.” This result could hamper nationwide momentum on demands that billionaires pay their fair share and states enacting new laws to tax the ultra-wealthy, but supporters say the fact that a proposed billionaire tax even made the ballot is a win. “While we hoped for Prop 40’s passage, this moment still marks progress toward a new era of bold taxation, and the billionaires know it,” said Nabil Ahmed, Oxfam America’s senior director of economic justice. “Over the course of the past few weeks and months we have seen popularity for taxing wealth grow, along with ever-strengthened support for its economic credibility.” Prop 40 proposed a one-time 5% tax on all individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1bn as of 1 January 2026. It was sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), and dictated that the proceeds from the tax would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance. The state’s leading unions, and progressive politicians such as Bernie Sanders, the Vermont senator, and Ro Khanna, a California congressman, backed Prop 40. But the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations such as Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, opposed it – pointing to its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. Prop 40’s most vocal critics, however, were the state’s billionaires. Donors to the opposition campaign were a who’s who of Silicon Valley , including executives from Google, Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, was Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder, who contributed at least $132m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings. All told, the billionaires mounted a nearly $425m battle against Prop 40, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. Compromiso con el pueblo estadounidense English Imprimir Páginas relacionadas Administrar cuidadosamente los fondos encomendados a nuestra agencia: los CDC cumplen con la responsabilidad fiscal de toda la agencia y la supervisión de las apropiaciones, las adquisiciones, la asistencia y el manejo financiero de los fondos gubernamentales. Esto ayuda a la misión de salud pública de los CDC al garantizar la administración fiscal adecuada del dinero de los contribuyentes. Financiación de los CDC * Brindar un ambiente apto para el crecimiento y la integridad intelectual y personal: los CDC tienen la expectativa de que los empleados conozcan y cumplan los catorce principios de conducta ética para el personal de la rama ejecutiva. Estos principios ayudan a fomentar el desarrollo para que tanto la agencia como cada empleado avancen en las ciencias de salud pública y mantengan la confianza del público. Ética y actividades de cumplimiento * Fundamentar todas las decisiones de salud pública en información científica de la más alta calidad, obtenida abierta y objetivamente: los CDC se aseguran de que sus actividades científicas y de investigación, así como sus empleados, cumplan con diversos reglamentos, leyes y políticas federales con el fin de mantener el más alto nivel de integridad científica. “Mejorar la calidad, la integridad y el acceso a los conocimientos científicos de los CDC” es uno de los 4 pilares que la Oficina del Director Adjunto de Asuntos Científicos de los CDC considera una prioridad y responsabilidad. Integridad científica * Colocar los beneficios para la sociedad por encima de los beneficios para nuestra institución: los empleados de los CDC tienen prohibido participar en todo asunto que pudiera presentar un conflicto de interés o dar la apariencia de una actuación sesgada. Esto ayuda a garantizar que los CDC logren investigaciones científicas de la más alta calidad y trabajen para proteger la salud de la nación. Consideraciones éticas para las colaboraciones entre el sector público y el privado * Conflicto de intereses económicos * Tratar a todas las personas con dignidad, honestidad y respeto: los Principios de la práctica ética de la salud pública * están dirigidos principalmente a las instituciones públicas y a otras en los Estados Unidos que tengan una misión de salud pública explícita.
