pages.text: Closing the Loop on Spinal Surgery | National Geographic Paid Content for Medtronic SCIENCE Closing the Loop on Spinal Surgery The complexity of spinal surgery can make treatment feel daunting. Now, connected technologies are helping create more predictable outcomes. 14:06 The spine’s intricate structure requires the most advanced approaches to surgical repair. video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated August 17, 2026 For centuries, every breakthrough in surgery has pursued the same goal: giving patients a better chance of recovery. From anaesthesia and antiseptics, to medical imaging and new, minimally invasive techniques—each innovation has helped surgeons operate with greater confidence and precision. Yet, despite remarkable advances, one challenge has remained: variability. Every patient is different, every procedure is unique, and even the most experienced surgeons must navigate countless decisions before, during, and after the operating room. Nowhere is this variability more evident than in spinal surgery. The human spine is one of the body's most intricate structures, meaning that no two procedures are ever the same. Success depends not only on surgical skill, but on careful planning, execution, and informed decision-making throughout the entire patient journey. From diagnosis to recovery. For decades, every stage of spinal surgery has been shaped by countless clinical decisions. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions For surgical teams, making the right decisions at every stage is a constant responsibility. For patients, this uncertainty can make the prospect of treatment feel daunting. Sean Phinney, who features in our video, explains: “Like many people, I think I was very afraid of what a significant back surgery might mean.” Historically, the pre-operative, intraoperative, and post-operative stages of surgery have existed as separate parts of the process, with spinal alignment often only confirmed through post-operative imaging. Today, for patients like Sean and many more, AI-powered technologies are helping spinal surgery become a more connected and intelligent process. Connected technologies are bringing pre-op, operative, and post-op stages of care into a single workflow. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions Medtronic is one company that is driving this shift. Through its AiBLE™ Smart Ecosystem, the health tech organization has successfully brought together planning, navigation, implants, and outcomes into a single workflow. Before surgery even begins, full-body imaging and AI-powered planning tools allow surgeons to create a personalized blueprint based on each patient's unique anatomy. Then, in the operating room, robotics and navigation technologies ensure precision while keeping clinical judgement firmly in human hands. In addition, patient-specific rods and real-time tracking enable surgeons to validate spinal alignment during the procedure, rather than waiting for post-operative X-rays. Medtronic’s goal is to close the loop across the surgical journey for better outcomes all round. Not only does AiBLE™ help reduce variability and improve the predictability of procedures, but it also lessens the cognitive load placed on surgeons, allowing them to focus more attention on the patient. As Vignesh Shetty, VP of AI & Product Development, reflects: “I wake up in the morning super stoked and excited about the possibility of making healthcare more personalized, more accessible, and higher quality.” Medtronic is helping advance the future of spinal surgery and connected healthcare. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions Perhaps the greatest power of innovations like AiBLE™ lies in their ability to continuously refine and scale surgical knowledge. Every procedure generates valuable information. As data from thousands of patients accumulates over time, it becomes a growing body of knowledge that can improve planning tools, workflows, and procedures. pages.description: BLM established a categorical exclusion to improve predictability and reduce burdens for companies seeking permits for wintertime oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska.
pages.text: BLM Streamlines Winter Exploration in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve | Bureau of Land Management Skip to main navigation Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn < All Press Releases BLM Streamlines Winter Exploration in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve Organization: Bureau of Land Management Media Contact: BLM Alaska Press BLM_AK_Press@blm.gov Oct 8, 2026 Ice Road in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. Photo by Charlie Ebbers, BLM ANCHORAGE, Alaska — Today, the Bureau of Land Management established a categorical exclusion to improve predictability and reduce burdens for companies seeking permits for wintertime oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. This action enables important winter exploration projects—such as exploratory seismic surveys, exploration wells, and plugging and abandonment— to move forward efficiently, advancing American Energy Dominance and national security. The BLM developed this categorical exclusion after analyzing the dozens of previous environmental assessments the agency has conducted for wintertime exploration in the Petroleum Reserve. Those analyses show that those exploration activities result in no significant impacts on human health or the environment when conducted under established operating procedures and mitigation measures. Wintertime exploration relies on temporary ice roads, ice pads, and snow routes where the only potential sign of exploration after the snow melts is generally the well-head, if drilled. “The BLM has decades of experience analyzing the effects of exploration in the Petroleum Reserve and permitting responsible exploration,” said BLM Alaska State Director Kevin Pendergast . “This categorical exclusion builds on that record to allow developers to more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve, ultimately increasing domestic energy supply, leading to stable energy costs and more revenue for Alaskan communities and the American public.” Categorical exclusions are categories of actions that have been determined to not typically result in significant environmental impacts, eliminating the need conduct a full environmental review. Streamlining National Environmental Policy Act compliance through categorical exclusions removes regulatory burdens and speeds up the process, saving time, and resources. Before relying on a categorical exclusion for a proposed project, an agency must verify that there are no extraordinary circumstances, such as potential impacts to endangered species or cultural resources, that may result in the project having any significant environmental effects. This new categorical exclusion supports the goals of Executive Order 14153, “Unleashing Alaska’s Extraordinary Resource Potential ,” Executive Order 14154, “Unleashing American Energy ,” and the Working Families Tax Cuts Act . The action builds on the BLM’s extensive work to improve regulatory certainty in the Petroleum Reserve, including rescission of the 2024 rule that restricted leasing and development in the Petroleum Reserve and reopening nearly 82% of the area to oil and gas leasing through an updated Integrated Activity Plan . It also complements BLM’s ongoing work to streamline permitting for qualifying production sites in the area. About 3.5 million acres are currently leased in the Petroleum Reserve following the historic lease sale held in March 2026. That sale resulted in 187 tracts receiving bids and $163,696,722 in total receipts, generating the most revenue ever, the most tracts receiving bids and the second most acreage sold in a single sale for the area. pages.description: Learn about USAGov's product principles, which help us evaluate our work in serving people and government agencies, and motivate our decisions.
pages.text: USAGov's product principles | USAGov Skip to main content USAGov's product principles Our product principles are the fundamental values that motivate our actions and decisions. They help us evaluate our work in serving people and government agencies. USAGov is the front door to a government by the people, of the people, for the people. We welcome people by: Building experiences that work on every screen, on every channel, in English and in Spanish Using assistive technologies to create complete, easy-to-navigate experiences for users Prioritizing the needs of people who have to rely on interacting directly with the government USAGov shows care for the people who use our service, especially when they are upset or facing painful circumstances. We demonstrate empathy for our users by: Helping people access our services in less-than-ideal situations, such as during financial hardship or after a natural disaster Stating clearly when USAGov cannot provide direct assistance Valuing and improving the experience of USAGov staff, so we can remain empathetic as we serve people who need help from the government USAGov empowers everyday people to navigate government. We empower people by: Helping users complete their tasks without taking away their decisions or independence Explaining what happens next, especially when users leave the USAGov environment Educating without patronizing, confusing, or minimizing USAGov is accountable for all of the information that we share with the public. We ensure accountability by: Collaborating across agencies to ensure the accuracy and consistency of content and advice. It is better to be incomplete than incorrect. Respecting the cultural differences between speakers of different languages, and never relying solely on literal translation to achieve the intent of a piece of content Accounting for the experience of every USAGov staff role that makes our service possible so they can be responsive to the needs of the public USAGov is a productivity tool, giving people fast, accurate service. We respect the people who use our services by: Delivering exactly what we say we will in each experience; neither under- nor over-promising Optimizing for the most common and important tasks, which change over time based on world events, policy, and circumstances Taking time to understand where we can build for a general audience, and where we should offer different paths for different needs USAGov is a steward of taxpayer resources. We display conscientious stewardship by: Partnering with other federal agencies to produce the most efficient experience for users Pursuing opportunities to make our resources available to other government agencies Demonstrating fiduciary responsibility in our choices and valuing staff efficiency LAST UPDATED: December 17, 2024 SHARE THIS PAGE: Have a question? Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office Subscribe for Office Updates Sign up to receive Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office news, events, our newsletter and funding opportunities. Subscribe The U.S. Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office (AFFO) enables research, development, and demonstration (RD&D) to accelerate technology commercialization for the production, storage, delivery and use of alternative fuels, fertilizers, chemicals, and feedstocks to enhance the security and reliability of energy networks and lower energy costs for Americans. Through collaboration with our National Laboratories, academia, and industry, AFFO advances energy independence by establishing a secure domestic supply chain, lowering production costs, invigorating a strong U.S. workforce, and fostering energy growth through diverse, domestic production pathways. As part of the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, AFFO integrates legacy efforts in the Bioenergy Technologies Office and Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Technologies Office under one office. AFFO focuses on: Cost-effective conversion of feedstocks to affordable chemicals and strategic fuels; Fuel-flexible fuel cells to provide prime and backup power for U.S. data centers and other growing electrical loads; Production of performance-enhanced chemicals to advance U.S. manufacturing dominance; Reduction of imported fertilizer by providing cost-effective domestic alternatives from hydrogen and biomass; and Leveraging growing use of super intelligence to spur innovation, advance technology readiness levels, and enable commercialization. Relevant Topics Funding Opportunities AFFO selects RD&D projects through open and competitive procurements, and encourages collaborative partnerships among: Industry Universities National laboratories Federal, state, and local governments Non-government agencies. pages.text: Disability Resources - Frequently Asked Questions | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Disability Resources - Frequently Asked Questions Question: Where can I get information about making workplace accommodations? Answer: The Job Accommodation Network (JAN) , sponsored by the Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), provides employers, employees and others information about appropriate accommodations for specific individuals and jobs. JAN also provides information on the employment provisions of the Americans with Disabilities Act and on resources for technical assistance, funding, education, training and services related to the employment of people with disabilities. JAN features the Searchable Online Accommodation Resource (SOAR) , a web-based database of accommodation information based on the more than 250,000 cases to which it has responded. JAN can also be reached at 800-526-7234 (voice and TTY). Category: Disability Resources Subcategory: Workplace Accommodations, Resources and Assistance Question: What percentage of people with disabilities are employed? Answer: The statistics vary depending on the source data and the definition of disability. The Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP) reports disability employment statistics from the Current Population Survey (CPS), which include three key statistics for people with and without disabilities: Labor force participation rate – the total labor force divided by the entire population Employment-population ratio – the number of people employed divided by the entire population Unemployment rate – the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force ODEP's disability employment statistics webpage also provides information on youth with disabilities, labor force statistics by disability status and race/ethnicity, and includes links to additional disability employment statistics resources. For breakdowns by state, ODEP publishes maps of the employment-population ratio for people with and without disabilities by state and race or ethnicity and median annual earnings by disability status, state, and sex . ODEP produces a series of Disability Data Blogs that focus on various topics such as the employment of people with disabilities in skilled trade professions. ODEP and their grantees, contractors, and other partners also undertake a variety of research, analysis, and evaluation efforts to help achieve the goal of increasing quality employment opportunities for people with disabilities, which are posted on ODEP's Current and Recently Completed Work and Past Research webpages. Category: Disability Resources: Disability Employment Data, Employment Statistics Subcategory Question: What can I do if I think my employer or supervisor is discriminating against me because of my disability? Answer: The Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP) has a helpful fact sheet, Employment Rights, Who Has Them and Who Enforces Them , which summarizes the federal laws that prohibit discrimination against people with disabilities and provides contact information for further information and assistance. There may also be applicable laws in your state. Contact your state Department of Labor office for more information. Category: Disability Resources Subcategory: Employment Discrimination, Disability Rights Question: How does the federal government define "disability"? Answer: The definition of "disability" varies depending on the purpose for which it is being used. MIT OpenCourseWare is a free and open collection of material from thousands of MIT courses, covering the entire MIT curriculum. Knowledge is your reward. Realizing this ideal is critical to enabling people to address global educational and societal challenges. Trustworthy Content in a Rapidly Changing Information Landscape As artificial intelligence and social media stretch the bounds of facts and truth, human insight and discernment are more important than ever. pages.title: اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه | الأمم المتحدة
pages.description: النفايات البشرية تنشر الأمراض القاتلة. ويُراد من اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه الدفع للعمل على معالجة أزمة الصرف الصحي العالمية.
pages.text: اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه | الأمم المتحدة Skip to main content فتيات يتشاركن لحظة من الفرح. يسلّط اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه 2026 الضوء على أهمية توفير خدمات صرف صحي مأمونة ومنصفة للجميع. Photo: © يونيسف/Brandon Lopez دورات مياه آمنة. مستقبل منصف يركز اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه 2026 على الصرف الصحي والمساواة بين الجنسين. وتبيّن حملة «دورات مياه آمنة. مستقبل منصف» كيف يحمي الصرف الصحي المأمون صحة النساء والفتيات وسلامتهن وكرامتهن وفرصهن، بما يتيح لهن التعلّم والعمل والمشاركة الكاملة في المجتمع. كيف تسهم دورات المياه في تحقيق المساواة بين الجنسين؟ حين تتوافر للفتيات والنساء دورات مياه آمنة ومأمونة، إلى جانب الصابون والمياه ومرافق النظافة الصحية أثناء فترة الطمث، تتمكن الفتيات من التعلّم والنساء من كسب الرزق. وفي المستشفيات والعيادات، تحمي خدمات الصرف الصحي والنظافة الصحية المريضات والعاملات في مجال الرعاية الصحية، وتسهم في تحسين النتائج الصحية للجميع. وفي الأماكن العامة، من الأسواق إلى مراكز النقل، تعزز دورات المياه قدرة النساء والفتيات على التنقل والاستقلال والمشاركة. كيف تؤثر أزمة الصرف الصحي في النساء والفتيات؟ يعيش 3.4 مليار شخص محرومين من خدمات الصرف الصحي المأمونة، غير أن وطأة الأزمة لا تقع على الجميع بالقدر نفسه. ويفاقم الحرمان من الصرف الصحي المأمون غياب المساواة بين الجنسين، إذ يعرّض النساء والفتيات للأمراض والمخاطر وسوء المعاملة، ويمس حقوقهن في الصحة والتعليم والعمل. ويؤدي استخدام دورات مياه غير نظيفة أو معطلة، أو الاضطرار إلى قضاء الحاجة في العراء، إلى الوصم والشعور بالعار، بما يزعزع ثقة النساء والفتيات بأنفسهن وشعورهن بالأمان. ويزيد تغير المناخ والظواهر الجوية المتطرفة أزمة الصرف الصحي تفاقما في مناطق كثيرة؛ وعندما تتعطل الخدمات، تتحمل النساء والفتيات العبء الأكبر. كيف نضمن أن تعني دورات المياه الآمنة مستقبلا منصفا؟ يجب أن تكون النساء شريكات في صياغة حلول الصرف الصحي، وأن يعملن جنبا إلى جنب مع الرجال على تصميم الخدمات وإدارتها وتقديمها بما يلبي احتياجات الجميع. وتُعد مشاركة النساء والفتيات وسائر الفئات التي تتأثر على نحو غير متناسب بالصرف الصحي غير المأمون، بمن فيهم كبار السن والأشخاص ذوو الإعاقة والأشخاص ذوو الهويات الجنسانية المتنوعة، شرطا أساسيا لبناء خدمات قادرة على الصمود لا تترك أحدا خلف الركب. ويتعين الاستثمار في خدمات الصرف الصحي المراعية للمنظور الجنساني، وجعل دورات المياه قوة دافعة للمساواة تعود بالنفع على الجميع، في كل مكان، دون تمييز. ما الخطوة التي ستتخذونها في اليوم العالمي لدورات المياه 2026؟ نزّلوا الموارد وألهموا العمل. وساهموا في إذكاء الوعي بالصلة بين الصرف الصحي والمساواة بين الجنسين. الموارد الرسائل الرئيسية لليوم العالمي لدورات المياه 2026 الصرف الصحي ركيزة للمساواة بين الجنسين. تحمي دورات المياه الآمنة صحة النساء والفتيات وسلامتهن وكرامتهن وفرصهن، بما يتيح لهن التعلّم والعمل والمشاركة الكاملة في المجتمع. تمس أزمة الصرف الصحي الجميع، ولكن آثارها لا تقع عليهم بالقدر نفسه. يفاقم الصرف الصحي الخطر غياب المساواة بين الجنسين بتعريض النساء والفتيات للأمراض والمخاطر وسوء المعاملة، ويمس حقوقهن في الصحة والتعليم والعمل. الصرف الصحي المأمون حق عالمي من حقوق الإنسان. فعندما تعجز خدمات الصرف الصحي عن تلبية احتياجات نصف السكان، تتعطل قدرة مجتمعات بأكملها على التقدم. دورات المياه الآمنة تعني مستقبلا منصفا. يجب أن تكون النساء شريكات في صياغة حلول الصرف الصحي لضمان أن تلبي الخدمات احتياجات الجميع، فتغدو دورات المياه قوة دافعة للمساواة تعود بالنفع على الجميع، في كل مكان، دون تمييز. وقائع وأرقام يفتقر 4 من كل 10 أشخاص في العالم، أي 3.4 مليار شخص، إلى دورات مياه آمنة. ( منظمة الصحة العالمية/يونيسف، 2025 ) يفتقر شخص واحد من كل 5 أشخاص، أي 1.7 مليار شخص، إلى مكان في المنزل لغسل اليدين بالماء والصابون. ( منظمة الصحة العالمية/يونيسف، 2025 ) تضطر واحدة من كل 5 مراهقات تتراوح أعمارهن بين 10 و19 عاما إلى مشاركة دورات مياه تفتقر إلى الشروط الصحية مع أسر أخرى أو إلى قضاء الحاجة في العراء. ( منظمة الصحة العالمية/يونيسف، 2023 ) في 79 بلدا، تشغل النساء أقل من نصف الوظائف الحكومية في قطاع المياه والصرف الصحي والنظافة الصحية؛ وفي 23 بلدا يشغلن أقل من وظيفة واحدة من كل 10 وظائف. ( منظمة الصحة العالمية/لجنة الأمم المتحدة المعنية بالموارد المائية، 2022 ) تتوافر صناديق للتخلص من نفايات فترة الطمث في دورات مياه الفتيات في أقل من مدرسة واحدة من كل 3 مدارس على مستوى العالم. ( منظمة الصحة العالمية/يونيسف، 2024 ) المواضيع السابقة لل

Historia de los CDC Inglés (English) Imprimir Páginas relacionadas El 1 de julio de 1946 se abrió el Centro de Enfermedades Contagiosas ( Communicable Disease Center , CDC) en un piso de un pequeño edificio en Atlanta. Su misión principal era simple, aunque sumamente exigente: prevenir que el paludismo (malaria) se propagara por todo el país. Contando con un presupuesto de solo 10 millones de dólares y menos de 400 empleados, los primeros retos de la agencia incluyeron obtener suficientes camiones, rociadores y palas necesarios para desatar la guerra contra los mosquitos. Como la organización echó raíces en el sur, conocido alguna vez como el corazón de la zona del paludismo (malaria), el fundador de los CDC, el Dr. Joseph Mountin, continuó abogando por los problemas de salud pública y presionando a los CDC para que extendieran sus responsabilidades a otras enfermedades contagiosas. En 1947, los CDC hicieron un pago simbólico de $10 a la Universidad de Emory por 15 acres de tierra en Clifton Road en Atlanta donde ahora funciona la sede principal de los CDC. Hoy, los CDC son uno de los componentes principales de operación del Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos, y se reconocen como la agencia principal del país para la promoción de la salud, la prevención y la preparación. Presente y futuro Los CDC celebraron su sexagésimo aniversario en 2006. Hoy en día, los CDC son la primera agencia de promoción de la salud, prevención y preparación del país y una agencia líder mundial en el área de la salud pública. La agencia sigue a la vanguardia de los esfuerzos de salud pública destinados a prevenir y controlar las enfermedades crónicas e infecciosas, las lesiones, los riesgos ocupacionales, las discapacidades y las amenazas para la salud. Los CDC son reconocidos en todo el mundo por sus estudios y trabajos de investigación así como por ser una agencia orientada a la acción. Los CDC realizan actividades de investigación y aplican los resultados de esos estudios para mejorar la vida diaria de las personas y responder a las emergencias de salud; esta es una característica que los diferencia de otras agencias similares. Los CDC trabajan con los estados y otros socios para ofrecer un sistema de vigilancia de salud con el fin de monitorizar y prevenir brotes de enfermedades (incluso las relacionadas con el terrorismo biológico), implementar estrategias de prevención de enfermedades y mantener estadísticas nacionales de salud. Los CDC también realizan esfuerzos a nivel internacional contra la transmisión de enfermedades, para lo cual cuentan con personal en más de 25 países. La atención de los CDC se concentra actualmente en el logro de las cuatro metas fundamentales para la protección de la salud, con el fin de convertirse en una agencia de resultados concretos cuyo énfasis especial sea la gente sana, los lugares saludables, la preparación y la salud global. Los CDC son uno de los 13 componentes principales del Departamento de Salud y Servicios Humanos (HHS). (en inglés) Última revisión: el 4 de junio del 2014 Fuente: Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn A Paw-powered Legacy Feb 23, 2026 Sled dogs will be nearly leaping out of their harnesses with excitement as they wait to take off for the Iditarod Ceremonial Start in downtown Anchorage as they do every March. Once moving, the teams traverse an 11-mile route to their finish on BLM’s Campbell Tract , where they are greeted by enthusiastic onlookers waiting to see the teams emerge from the woods. Topo the sled dog. NPS photo by L. Wise. When it comes to sled dogs, nothing is more iconic than the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race—an annual event where mushers and their teams brave more than 1,000 miles of trails, including portions of the Iditarod National Historic Trail , from Willow to Nome, Alaska. The Bureau of Land Management plays a unique role as administrator of the Iditarod National Historic Trail, working with agencies and partners to cooperatively manage the 2,000+ mile trail system. Each year, BLM Alaska also welcomes guests to the Iditarod Ceremonial Start, a festive precursor to the race, where visitors can cheer on mushers and their dogs along part of the race route. As we prepare for the exciting race season, it got us wondering: What does mushing look like across Alaska’s vast public lands? And better yet—what does it look like through the eyes of a dog? We knew we had to get answers to our burning questions, so we reached out to a friend who knows mushing better than most: Denali National Park and Preserve ’s very own Bark Ranger, Topo . The Denali Sled Dog Kennel was established over a century ago, 104 years to be exact. The dogs were one of the first purchases made by the park’s employee, Harry Karstens. In the 1920s, dog teams were the most reliable and efficient way to travel through Interior Alaska. These first dog teams played a vital role in shaping the park: they helped establish its boundaries, hauled supplies to build patrol cabins, and put an end to market hunting of wildlife in the newly protected park. Today, the sled dogs continue to support park management and protection, but they also serve as beloved ambassadors. They connect visitors to the park’s history and educate the public about the tradition of dogsledding—a practice that has been part of Denali for a century and is rooted in a 10,000-year-old cultural heritage of the North. Topo leading the sled dog team on a patrol in Denali. NPS Photo by Ashley Guevara. BLM: Well, hello, Topo! We understand your way of greeting might be a bit different than ours—mind if we stick to a paw shake? Topo: Absolutely, put it here, my friend. BLM: We’ve heard you’ve run almost 12,000 miles on patrol in Denali National Park and Preserve. That’s incredible! Topo: Thank you very much. Yes, that’s a lot of miles on these paws. BLM: How do you train for your winter patrols? Topo: Each fall my canine ranger friends and I all start running short distances, pulling a wheeled cart around the campground at the park. And each week we run a little farther and a little farther the following week. As freighting sled dogs, our aim is to build up our strength, pull heavy loads, and be able to comfortably run about 20-30 miles per day. BLM: Do you have a favorite memory from your winter patrols? Topo: I’d have to say that some of my favorite memories are the patrols on the western side of the park, out near Wonder Lake. We typically don’t get there until March, when the sun is shining a little more, and on the clear days the mountain views are just outstanding. pages.description: Andy Biggs wins nomination to challenge Katie Hobbs as Alex Kolodin won party’s primary for secretary of state
pages.text: Election deniers win Republican primaries in Arizona | Arizona | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Andy Biggs speaks to the media during his primary election night watch party in Scottsdale, Arizona. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters View image in fullscreen Andy Biggs speaks to the media during his primary election night watch party in Scottsdale, Arizona. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters Arizona This article is more than 3 months old Election deniers win Republican primaries in Arizona This article is more than 3 months old Andy Biggs wins nomination to challenge Katie Hobbs as Alex Kolodin won party’s primary for secretary of state Lauren Gambino Wed 22 Jul 2026 15.49 EDT First published on Tue 21 Jul 2026 23.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump-backed candidates in Arizona prevailed in key primary contests on Tuesday, setting up a fall campaign that will test whether Republicans can reverse some of their recent losses in the presidential battleground state. Andy Biggs, the hard-right congressman endorsed by Donald Trump, easily won the Republican nomination to challenge the incumbent Democrat, Governor Katie Hobbs. The race is expected to be among the most fiercely contested in the country, with control of the governor’s office carrying outsized national significance in a state that became “ground zero” for election denialism after Trump’s narrow loss there in 2020. Biggs, a former chair of the House Freedom caucus who was a central figure in the effort to overturn Trump’s election defeat, trounced fellow congressman David Schweikert, by appealing to the party’s deeply conservative base. Hobbs, who flipped the seat from red to blue in 2022, ran unopposed. Alex Kolodin, a Republican state representative and attorney who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, also won the party’s primary to become its secretary of state: Arizona’s top election official. Kolodin will face the Democratic incumbent, Adrian Fontes, in November for the office that will oversee elections in a swing state during the 2028 presidential race. Fontes has cast himself as a bulwark against Trump’s election denialism, while overseeing elections in one of the nation’s most closely watched battleground states. Arizona’s Republican elections brawl raises fears over midterms, denialism and Trump: ‘The biggest threat is the president’ Read more In an all-caps social media post on Wednesday, Trump declared “A COMPLETE SWEEP!!!” “MAGA CANDIDATES WON EVERYTHING LAST NIGHT IN ARIZONA,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He added: “AFTER DECADES, ARIZONA IS BECOMING A REPUBLICAN STATE.” In fact, Arizona was long a Republican stronghold and only recently transformed into a competitive swing state, fueled by rapid population growth, shifting suburban voting patterns around Phoenix and an influx of college-educated voters. In the decade since Trump’s 2016 election, Arizona Democrats have gained control of the top three statewide offices – governor, attorney general and secretary of state – as well as both US Senate seats. But Trump still narrowly carried Arizona in 2024 after losing the state four years earlier – a shock defeat he unsuccessfully sought to overturn. Throughout the Republican gubernatorial campaign, Biggs and Schweikert offered contrasting visions for reclaiming the governorship. Schweikert, who gave up his toss-up congressional seat to run for governor after eight terms, argued that Biggs’s hard-right politics and unswerving embrace of the president had allowed Democrats to make gains in once-ruby-red Arizona. pages.text: Disability Employment Statistics | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Disability Employment Statistics Credible, consistent data is critical to creating change. ODEP promotes the availability and use of disability data and statistics to further education, research, and policy initiatives to improve employment opportunities and outcomes for people with disabilities. This work was first revealed in 2008, when after several years of research and testing, new questions were added to the monthly Current Population Survey (CPS) to gauge the employment status of people with disabilities. The questions, which were originally developed for use in the American Community Survey (ACS), were added after extensive collaboration between ODEP, DOL's Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and other stakeholders, and were sponsored by ODEP. Prior to this, there was no way to measure the labor force status of people with disabilities on a regular basis. Today, these data are updated monthly, providing citizens and policymakers with reliable and accurate information on a topic of importance to America's workforce and economy. Disability Labor Force Statistics These statistics are obtained directly from BLS publication of monthly aggregate series derived from the Current Population Survey (CPS) and are not seasonally-adjusted. Annual averages are calculated over the 12 months of that calendar year, and 12-month moving averages (12m MAs) are calculated ending in the latest month for which data is available. The age range 16-64 is commonly considered to be the “working-age population”, while the age range 16 and older is the entire age range for which the CPS reports labor force data. “M” and “F” in the column headings indicate the data in that column is limited to men and women, respectively. pages.title: Connecting the Past and the Future | National Geographic
pages.description: Rome and New York City weren't built in a day. Discover how today's digital infrastructure is shaping the cities of yesterday and tomorrow.
pages.text: Connecting the Past and the Future | National Geographic Paid Content for Boldyn SCIENCE Connecting the Past and the Future Rome and New York City weren't built in a day. Discover how today's digital infrastructure is shaping the cities of yesterday and tomorrow. 12:23 The complexity of some cities’ architecture makes modernization a different kind of challenge entirely. Video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent Last updated August 12, 2026 Cities are constantly evolving. They are built up, layer by layer, each generation leaving its mark on the one before. Roman roads became the foundation for medieval streets. Aqueducts gave way to railways, electricity, and underground transportation. Over time, every city’s infrastructure becomes a record of the people who shaped it years before. Walk through Rome, and the history is impossible to ignore. Ancient walls sit beside modern apartments; the remains of a long-gone empire lie under busy streets. Layers of the past can be felt everywhere: yet Rome, just like every great city, cannot stand still. Today, millions of visitors and residents move through the city, expecting to stay connected above and below ground. From GPS and wayfinding tools to digital tickets and tap-to-pay features for transport systems, to instant communication between families and friends. The challenge is that today’s expectations for connectivity must be woven into yesterday’s infrastructure, without damaging what lies beneath. After all, every small hole dug for cabling can become an entire archaeological event. One of Boldyn's greatest challenges is that making even the smallest hole can uncover historical ruins or artefacts. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions NYC faces its own unique complexities. The city is built on a network of century-old, concrete-walled subway tunnels, designed for transporting commuters, not enabling video calling and streaming services through tunnels deep underground. For the city that never sleeps, and the network that supports over 1 billion riders annually, suspending service in tunnels is a challenging task. Two cities, separated by history, geography, and culture. Yet, both Rome and NYC demand the answer to the same question: How do you thread connectivity through places that weren’t designed to carry it? The NYC subway was designed to move people, not data. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions To answer this question, both cities turned to Boldyn Networks (Boldyn). Specializing in designing, deploying and enabling digital infrastructure in some of the world's most complex environments, the company works behind the scenes to bring reliable and future-ready connectivity to places where conventional approaches won't work. In Rome, this means respecting a UNESCO World Heritage Site and all its restrictions, and in NYC this means installing network infrastructure in one of the world’s largest, busiest, and most complex subway systems that runs twenty-four seven. Building digital infrastructure in historic cities requires more than technical expertise. It demands an understanding that every new development must coexist with the ones before: Supporting the future, without destroying the past. As Antonino Ruggiero, CEO of Italy & Spain, puts it, a key concern at every stage of modernization is making sure that cities are “preserved and respected.” Central to this approach is Boldyn's Neutral Host model. Rather than every mobile operator building its own infrastructure, the model allows a single shared infrastructure to be built, which multiple wireless carriers then join. The result is a more efficient, sustainable solution that reduces disruption, minimizes construction, and helps prepare cities for the future. For Boldyn, delivering modern connectivity means working around a system that rarely stops running. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions Boldyn has unique expertise in deploying connectivity solutions across some of the world's busiest and most complex environments. F

pages.title: 世界厕所日 | 联合国
pages.description: 为了帮助打破关于厕所的禁忌，并让人人享有环境卫生成为全球发展的优先事项，联合国大会指定11月19日为世界厕所日。
pages.text: 世界厕所日 | 联合国 Skip to main content 图片 儿基会/Brandon Lopez 安全厕所，平等未来 2026年世界厕所日聚焦卫生设施与性别平等。本次宣传活动以“ 安全厕所，平等未来 ”为主体，阐明安全的卫生设施如何保障妇女和女童的健康、安全、尊严与发展机会，助力妇女和女童就学、就业，并充分参与社会生活。 厕所如何促进性别平等？ 若能使用安全可靠的厕所，还有肥皂、水和经期卫生设施，女童就可以安心学习，妇女也能赚取收入。 在医院和诊所，环境卫生和个人卫生服务保护着妇女患者和医疗照护工作者，提供更好的健康成果，惠及所有人。 从市场到交通枢纽等公共场所，厕所守护着妇女和女童的出行、独立和社会参与。 卫生设施危机如何影响妇女和女童？ 全球有34亿人缺乏安全的卫生设施，但人们受到的影响各不相同。 无法获取安全卫生设施会加剧性别不平等，使妇女和女童面临疾病、人身危险与侵害风险，进而损害妇女和女童的健康权、受教育权与劳动权。 使用不干净或损坏的厕所，或者不得不在户外排便，会产生病耻感和羞愧感，影响妇女和女童的自信心和安全感。 气候变化和极端天气事件造成许多地区的卫生设施危机愈演愈烈，一旦卫生服务中断，妇女和女童将首当其冲。 如何让安全厕所构筑人人平等的未来？ 妇女必须参与制定卫生设施解决方案，与男性协同合作，共同设计、管理并提供惠及全体民众的服务。 妇女、女童、老年人、残障人士、性别多元群体等受不安全卫生设施冲击更大的群体，必须参与其中，才能打造有韧性、普惠全民的卫生服务。 各国必须加大投入，建设兼顾性别需求的卫生设施，让厕所成为推动平等的有力抓手，在世界各地无歧视地造福所有民众。 2026年世界厕所日，你会采取什么行动？ 下载宣传资源，开启行动。推动安全厕所成为促进平等的力量，惠及每个人、每个地方，不带任何歧视。 相关资源 2026年世界厕所日核心信息 卫生设施是性别平等的基石。 安全的厕所能够保障妇女和女童的健康、安全、尊严与发展机会，让她们得以正常就学、就业，充分参与社会生活。 卫生设施危机影响所有人，但影响程度并不相同。 不安全的卫生设施会加剧性别不平等，使妇女和女童面临疾病、人身危险与侵害风险，进而损害妇女和女童的健康权、受教育权与劳动权。 安全的卫生设施是一项世界人权。 当卫生服务无法满足半数人口的需求时，整个社区的发展都会受到制约。 安全的厕所意味着平等的未来。 必须吸纳妇女参与卫生设施解决方案的规划，确保相关服务适配所有人的需求，让厕所成为推动平等的力量，在世界各地无歧视地造福每一个人。 你知道吗？ 全球十分之四的人口（34亿人）仍然无法获得安全的厕所。（ 世卫组织/儿基会，2025年 ） 全球五分之一的人口（17亿人）家中没有地方可使用肥皂和清水洗手。（ 世卫组织/儿基会，2025年 ） 五分之一的青春期少女（10-19岁）不得不与许多其他家庭共用不卫生的厕所，或露天如厕。（ 世卫组织/儿基会，2023年 ） 在接受问卷统计的79个国家中，妇女在政府水务环卫岗位任职人数占比不足半数；此外，还有23个国家报告称，妇女在上述岗位的占比不到十分之一。（ 世卫组织/联合国水机制，2022年 ） 全球范围内，仅有不到三分之一的学校在女厕配备生理期废弃物收纳箱。（ 世卫组织/儿基会，2024年 ） 往届世界厕所日主题 浏览 联合国水机制关于世界厕所日宣传活动的档案 ，回顾自2014年以来的各项活动， 其内容涵盖气候、废水、基于自然的解决方案及和平等主题。 联合国水机制 ：协调联合国在水和环境卫生方面的工作 联合国没有一个专门机构单独负责水问题。超过30个联合国机构正在执行水和环境卫生项目，这反映出，水问题贯穿了联合国的所有重要领域。联合国水机制负责协调各方，以便联合国大家庭在应对有关水问题的挑战时采取“一体行动”。 2026年联合国世界水发展报告 2026年联合国世界水发展报告《 人人享有水 , 平等权利与机会 》揭示了性别不平等如何影响全球水与卫生危机并受其影响，并提出了旨在推动进展的包容性及兼顾性别视角的应对方案。 我们为什么要纪念国际日？ 国际日和国际周 是提高公众对有关问题的认识、调动政治意愿和资源应对全球性问题以及庆祝和加强人类成就的机会。国际日在联合国成立之前就已经存在，但联合国将国际日作为一种有力的宣传工具。 了解更多>>

pages.title: UNESCO : Building Peace through Education, Science and Culture, communication and information
pages.description: Learn more about UNESCO's role, vision and results. UNESCO is the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Our aim is to promote peace and security through international cooperation
pages.text: UNESCO : Building Peace through Education, Science and Culture, communication and information Skip to main content Help Us Improve Your UNESCO Website Experience close Search Search Quick links: AI Response to Crisis Key Challenges ©Ramon R/Shutterstock.com COP31: Protecting our water reserves As COP31 takes place in Antalya, Türkiye (9-20 November 2026) on the theme of water and ocean resilience, UNESCO advocates for integrated solutions combining science, education and Indigenous and local knowledge. With glaciers, ice and snow, which hold nearly 70% of the world’s freshwater, melting rapidly, UNESCO is also releasing a report on how AI shapes our understanding of climate change. Read more 80 years in the service of peace On 4 November 1946, UNESCO's Constitution entered into force. Eighty years ago, an organization was born from a simple conviction: that peace is built in the minds of women and men, through knowledge, dialogue and cooperation. Since then, UNESCO has set international standards, protected heritage, defended freedom of expression, supported education and put science at the service of humanity. Relive the voices and moments that shaped its history, alongside its 194 Member States. Read more © UNESCO Delivering for people in crisis Culture, education, science, and information are essential needs in times of turbulence and crisis. They are powerful drivers of social cohesion, resilience, and hope in a better future. UNESCO plays a vital role in safeguarding the social and cultural foundations that underpin stability, dignity, and recovery for communities affected by crises. By protecting these pillars, we help ensure that societies can rebuild not only infrastructure, but also trust, identity, and the collective capacity to move forward. Read more ©UNESCO Our impact in communities Discover how UNESCO drives change around the world. How youth drafted an agenda for education beyond 2030 University of Juba students prepare to take first campus community radio station on air UNESCO World Heritage Series Season 4 - Korea: a journey through time Uganda Validates Five Strategic Frameworks aimed at Shaping the country's Future of STEM Education Load more UNESCO in brief UNESCO is the United Nations organization that promotes cooperation in education, science, culture and communication to foster peace worldwide. The Organization provides key services for its Member States, setting global norms and standards, developing tools for international cooperation, producing knowledge for public policies and building global networks of sites and institutions inscribed on its lists. Discover Thumbnail play_arrow © UNESCO Our fields of expertise UNESCO uses education, science, culture, communication and information to foster mutual understanding and respect for our planet. Our strategic objectives UNESCO's strategy addresses global challenges with goals in education, the environment, social cohesion, and technology. Delivering in times of emergencies UNESCO supports communities affected by conflict and natural disasters, ensuring access to quality education and safeguarding cultural heritage. Building stronger multilateralism UNESCO stands on the frontline of international cooperation, in close coordination with sister agencies of the UN System. UNESCO lists and designations UNESCO sites connect the world and highlight the best of our shared humanity. 1273 World Heritage Sites 849 Intangible Cultural Heritage 797 Biosphere Reserves 241 Global Geoparks Magazine: The UNESCO Courier UNESCO at 80 On 4 November 1946, UNESCO’s Constitution entered into force. Eighty years later, the Organization continues to pursue its foundational mission: building peace through education, science, culture, and information. But what does this ideal mean in today’s world, faced with unprecedented challenges? In this anniversary issue, The UNESCO Courier revisits eight decades of commitment and achievements. From lives transformed by education to heritage

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Using science to uncover mysteries of the Mesa archaeological site in Alaska Dec 18, 2025 North of the Arctic Circle, a solitary mesa rises abruptly from the Alaskan landscape just outside the National Petroleum Reserve. If you stood at the top today, you’d get an unobstructed, 360-degree view of the surrounding treeless tundra. Between roughly 11,700 and 13,600 years ago, Indigenous Inupiaq hunters found this same view useful for spotting Ice Age mammals – steppe bison, musk ox, and caribou – that roamed the landscape below. The people who occupied the mesa were some of North America’s early inhabitants, and they left behind thousands of artifacts and important features that tell a story about past activities at the site. These include stone projectile points that were probably mounted on lance-like spears and the remnants of 40 ancient campfires, referred to as "hearths" by archaeologists. Bureau of Land Management archaeologists discovered these artifacts in 1978 when they were surveying public lands here prior to oil exploration. Today, the artifacts reside at the University of Alaska Museum of the North in Fairbanks. Excavator working at the Mesa archaeological site in the Central Arctic Management Area Wilderness Study Area. Prior excavation and ongoing interpretation of archaeological resources at the Mesa site showcase the BLM’s multiple-use land management mission in action. For example, the BLM collaborates with Indigenous peoples to ensure respectful co-stewardship while managing public lands for multiple uses, such as energy development in the adjacent National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. In addition, new scientific findings at cultural sites deepen the public’s connections to the land they call home – where rich history and tradition bring these landscapes to life. Joe Keeney, archaeologist for the BLM Alaska Arctic District Office, elaborates on the findings at the Mesa site. According to Keeney, the hearths here contained charcoal, which being organic, can be radiocarbon dated. “Being recovered from the same ancient layer of sediment, the hearths and stone points were found in the same context, so the stone points can be dated indirectly using the dated charcoal in the hearths,” explains Keeney. Using accelerator mass spectrometry, which allows accurate and reliable dating, archaeologists determined that some of the artifacts from the Mesa site were nearly 12,000 years old, making the site among some of the oldest known archaeological sites in Alaska. Fast forward to present day, and scientific technology is working to uncover new clues about the lifestyles of the people who occupied the mesa. Stormy Fields, a scientist at the Alaska Stable Isotope Facility at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, has questions about the people who occupied the site that she is hoping her research will answer. Fields is conducting a process called stable isotope analysis on the hearth sediments. "While we know that the Mesa people most likely used the site to look for large game millennia ago, there is potential for modern scientific technologies to shed additional light on their lifestyle from the ancient hearth features they left behind," said Fields. Fields explained that most of the radiocarbon dates from the hearths overlap with the relatively cold, dry time called the Younger Dryas (~11,000-10,000 years Before Present), a time which included a rapid shift in the climate that could have had an impact on available animal populations. pages.description: From North Carolina to Arizona, Democrats with almost no public profile were stunned at their election triumphs
pages.text: ‘Wait, what?’: the underdog Democrats who won their midterm races against all odds | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation LaKesha Womack: ‘I wanted to run a different type of race. I wanted to be more present in the community.’ Photograph: Kristian Womack View image in fullscreen LaKesha Womack: ‘I wanted to run a different type of race. I wanted to be more present in the community.’ Photograph: Kristian Womack US midterm elections 2026 ‘Wait, what?’: the underdog Democrats who won their midterm races against all odds From North Carolina to Arizona, Democrats with almost no public profile were stunned at their election triumphs Sam Levin Sat 7 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 06.41 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One candidate had dropped out in September. One had no campaign staff. One was a 19-year-old and halfway through the fall college semester. Across the US, Democratic candidates with almost no public profile and long odds of winning their midterm races were stunned to find they had outperformed their opponents on Tuesday. They were swept into Congress and statehouses in the blue wave that knocked out Republicans from seats considered untouchable in deep-red districts. “It’s very surreal,” said Victoria Broderick, a Tennessee Democrat poised to pull off an extraordinary upset in the state’s fourth congressional district, ousting Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais, who was seeking his ninth term. The prominent US election forecaster Cook Political Report rated it as a “solid Republican” district, and almost nobody in Washington thought Desjarlais could lose. Speaking on Wednesday after state officials declared she had won by about 300 votes, Broderick said: “I think the first words to my team were: ‘Wait, what?’ I was just sitting there shocked.” The Associated Press hasn’t yet called her race. In an indication of how eager some residents were to “vote blue no matter who”, Eric Armstrong, an Iowa Democrat, won his race for state representative despite having dropped out in early September. At the time, he cited “personal health issues that require my full attention and immediate care”. Even though Armstrong did not campaign for the last two months, he defeated Republican Keith Jones, a county supervisor and retired police lieutenant, by more than 800 votes . Armstrong didn’t respond to inquiries, but told the New York Times in a phone call on Wednesday morning: “I’m going to do my best to represent [the district] … But I still have health issues, that’s what I’m struggling with.” Jones said by phone Thursday that he was stunned by his loss: “It was a gut-punch. I worked really hard for eight months … the blue wave hit Iowa and Texas very hard, no doubt.” He said voters were concerned with the Iran war and gas prices – issues he couldn’t address as a state representative: “It’s hard to lose a race based on events outside of my control.” In Arizona, Sebastian Matta, a 19-year-old college student studying philosophy, defeated Jeff Dial, a 50-year-old Republican former state lawmaker, in the race to be Maricopa county clerk of the superior court. Matta told the Arizona Republic that he noticed Democrats had not run for the office in years : “I figured: ‘You know, why not?’” He said he expected it would be a “destined loss” for Democrats, but now he is set to lead the court’s clerk’s office for the nation’s fourth-largest county. View image in fullscreen Victoria Broderick Photograph: Victoria Broderick Campaign Some of the unexpected candidates weren’t prepared when they heard news of their success. In Tennessee, Broderick, the Democrat, worked a full-time job in tech support throughout her longshot campaign: “I’m a working-class mom. Process of Reviewing the National Ambient Air Quality Standards Process for Reviewing NAAQS Overview of the EPA’s Process for Reviewing the NAAQS (pdf) (2.37 MB) Sections 108 and 109 of the Clean Air Act (CAA) govern the establishment, review, and revision, as appropriate, of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for each criteria air pollutant to provide protection for the nation’s public health and the environment. The CAA requires periodic review of the science upon which the standards are based and the standards themselves. Reviewing the NAAQS is a lengthy undertaking and generally includes the following major phases: Planning Phase Each review begins with a public Call for Information to announce the initiation of a review and to solicit information on new scientific evidence and policy issues for consideration. The planning phase of the NAAQS review process may also include a science policy workshop, which is intended to gather input from the scientific community and the public regarding policy-relevant issues and questions that will frame the review. Drawing from the workshop discussions and public comments, EPA prepares an Integrated Review Plan (IRP) that conveys the schedule for the entire review, the process for conducting the review, and the key policy-relevant science issues that will guide the review. Process of Setting and Implementing NAAQS Standards - setting, reviewing, and revising the standards Designations - determining whether areas meet the standards Implementation - attaining and maintaining the standards Assessment Phase In the assessment phase, the EPA prepares the Integrated Science Assessment, Risk and Exposure Assessments (quantitative air quality, exposure and risk analyses), as warranted, and a Policy Assessment. Integrated Science Assessment (ISA) : This assessment is a comprehensive review, synthesis, and evaluation of the most policy-relevant science, including key science judgments that are important to inform the development of the risk and exposure assessments, as well as other aspects of the NAAQS review. Risk/Exposure Assessment (REA) : This assessment draws upon information and conclusions presented in the ISA to develop quantitative characterizations of exposures and associated risks to human health or the environment associated with air quality conditions estimated to just meet the current or alternative standard(s) under consideration. This assessment includes a characterization of the uncertainties associated with such estimates. Policy Assessment (PA): This assessment provides a transparent staff analysis of the scientific basis for alternative policy options for consideration by senior EPA management prior to rulemaking. Such an evaluation of policy implications is intended to help ‘‘bridge the gap’’ between the Agency’s scientific assessments, presented in the ISA and REA(s), and the judgments required of the EPA Administrator in determining whether it is appropriate to retain or revise the NAAQS. In so doing, the PA is also intended to facilitate the Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee’s (CASAC’s ) advice to the Agency and recommendations to the Administrator, as provided for in the CAA, on the adequacy of the existing standards or revisions that may be appropriate to consider. The PA focuses on the information that is most pertinent to evaluating the basic elements of the NAAQS: indicator, averaging time, form, and level. Scientific review during the development of these documents is thorough and extensive. Drafts of all documents are reviewed by CASAC and the public has an opportunity to comment

pages.title: Cooler Homes, Smarter Cities | National Geographic
pages.description: As climates change, our homes must too—and the future of comfort lies in balancing our needs with those of the world around us.
pages.text: Cooler Homes, Smarter Cities | National Geographic Paid Content for Carrier SCIENCE Cooler Homes, Smarter Cities As climates change, our homes must too—and the future of comfort lies in balancing our needs with those of the world around us. 14:12 Across the globe, air conditioning is becoming essential to how communities function. video by Nicely Done Productions By Sam Kent and Kelsey Taylor Last updated August 10, 2026 For more than a century, buildings have been designed to do one thing above all else—look after the people inside them. From schools and hospitals to offices and homes, comfortable indoor environments have enabled communities to live, work, and thrive. As the inventor of modern air conditioning, Carrier has helped shape that comfort for generations. Today, the challenge is evolving. As cities expand and temperatures rise, the buildings we depend on must do more than keep us comfortable. They must become more energy efficient, more intelligent, and better equipped to meet the demands of a changing world. "The future of comfort isn't simply about keeping homes cool," says Nick Arch, Vice President & General Manager, Residential Solutions at Carrier. "It's about creating homes that are intelligent enough to respond to both the needs of homeowners and the demands of the energy system around them." The question facing communities, planners, and technology leaders alike is no longer simply how to cool our homes and buildings. It’s how to do so in a way that supports a more sustainable and resilient energy future. Urban planners are rethinking how communities are built for a warmer world. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions The answer begins with rethinking the relationship between buildings and energy. For decades, homes have been designed to consume electricity when needed. Whether powering a stove, charging an electric vehicle, or cooling a living room on a hot summer afternoon, demand is largely dictated by the homeowner and met by the grid. But demand is not constant. On the hottest days and coldest nights, millions of homes draw power simultaneously, creating periods of peak demand that place significant strain on energy infrastructure. The U.S. electric grid has finite capacity, and expanding that capacity takes significant investment and time. As one of the country's largest providers of HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) solutions, Carrier understands both the importance of indoor comfort and the challenges associated with growing energy demand. The next generation of HVAC systems will be designed to balance comfort, efficiency, and environmental impact. Photograph by Nicely Done Productions Hakan Yilmaz, President of Carrier Energy and Chief Sustainability Officer, sees both the challenge and the opportunity. He explains that heating and cooling are among the country’s biggest uses of electricity, with Carrier itself representing approximately 100 gigawatts of load on the U.S. grid. This scale gives Carrier a unique opportunity to help shape how homes interact with the energy system of the future. As Hakan asserts: “We have an opportunity to make a meaningful impact by helping HVAC systems run more efficiently.” Rather than relying solely on building more power generation capacity, Carrier is helping lead a shift toward smarter energy management. The company's connected solutions are designed to make better use of existing electricity by intelligently adjusting energy consumption based on a home's needs and broader grid conditions. For homeowners, these adjustments often happen seamlessly in the background. Across millions of connected systems, however, the collective impact can be significant. It's a subtle but important shift in thinking. Homes and buildings are no longer just consumers of energy. Increasingly, they’re becoming active participants in the systems that power modern communities. Today’s challenges go beyond simply generating enough power. Photograph by Nicely Done Production

Anything I did prior wasn’t recorded, but I started mapping Chicago area roads and highways November 08, 2007. آیا چشمان شما سوزش دارد؟ Posted by Rezwan Eye Hospital on 15 November 2026 in Persian (فارسی) . آیا چشمان شما سوزش دارد؟ سوزش چشم، سرخی، خارش، خشکی و احساس خستگی ممکن است نشانه مشکلات مختلف چشمی باشد. بی‌توجهی به این علایم می‌تواند سلامت بینایی شما را تحت تأثیر قرار دهد. در مرکز تخصصی چشم رضوان، با معاینات دقیق و خدمات تخصصی، برای تشخیص علت ناراحتی‌های چشمی و انتخاب روش مناسب تداوی در کنار شما هستیم. سلامت چشمان‌تان را جدی بگیرید؛ برای معاینه تخصصی مراجعه کنید. شعبه کابل: کابل، دشت برچی، پل خشک، جوار شفاخانه عالمی، مارکیت توحید، منزل دوم تماس و واتساپ: 0773595032 | 0775713021 شعبه دایکندی: شهرک جدید نیلی، مارکیت شهر، زیر عزیزی‌بانک تماس: 0776680870 | 0778005008 وب‌سایت: www.rezwaneye.com مرکز تخصصی چشم رضوان؛ بینایی برای یک عمر مرکز_تخصصی_چشم_رضوان #سوزش_چشم #سلامت_چشم #معاینه_چشم #چشم_پزشکی Location: دشت برچی, ناحیه سیزدهم, كابل ښار, شاروالی کابل, ولایت کابل, 5000, افغانستان Capitole du Libre 2026 Posted by lhirlimann on 15 November 2026 in French (Français) . Hier soir, j’ai présenté dans l’amphithéâtre C002 au sein du campus de enseeiht à Toulouse, « Contribuez à OSM ». La bonne surprise fut le taux de remplissage de la salle. J’ai compté plus d’une vingtaine de personnes. La présentation était articulée en deux parties : la première, un tout petit peu de théorie et pas de présentation d’outils ; la deuxième, des démonstrations, des petits trucs faciles pour commencer, puis des trucs plus « grands » (de l’infrastructure). En trente minutes, j’avais plié ma présentation. Il restait vingt-cinq minutes, qui se sont très, très facilement remplies par de très nombreuses questions. Merci au plublic pour ces questions. Merci à l’organisation du Capitole du Libre. La présentation est disponible à https://files.hirlimann.net/talks/cdl2026/ . Location: Les Chalets / Bayard / Belfort / Saint-Aubin / Dupuy, Toulouse, Haute-Garonne, Occitanie, France métropolitaine, France Flow of the River Ilagan Posted by CodentGIS on 15 November 2026 in English . It’s been two months since I started to edit the Ilagan River again. While I had done so in the past, way before these two months, this period turned out to be a great adventure that I’m still hiking. It was a time after Project CaCau . When I put it to an end, I felt not only disappointed, but ambitious. Why exactly? Well, I don’t know, but the roaring engine I had used to keep me going through that project was still on, and I couldn’t just stop it. So, I had to redirect it somewhere. For a bit, I had just redirected it to OSM. I experimented with multiple things and tried to pick up my old stuff. But one in particular caught my attention. A while ago, I was editing the river area of the Ilagan River. I never picked it up again until then. Despite that, it just stuck. Starting in the 15th of September, I got into the flow of the edits, and I never stopped. I didn’t just do the main river either. I had also started doing its tributaries because my satisfaction didn’t get put with just that. I was now pushing 2K-3K edits a day, with the little free time I had. My satisfaction didn’t stop; I had also started mapping the landslide areas. Now, at that point, I was satisfied. La Fundación de los CDC English Imprimir Páginas relacionadas Recursos en Internet Fundación de los CDC * Blog y redes sociales * La Fundación de los CDC, que fue establecida por el Congreso como una organización independiente, sin fines de lucro, es la única entidad autorizada por el Congreso para movilizar socios filantrópicos y recursos del sector privado con el fin de respaldar la misión fundamental de los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades de proteger la salud. La Fundación de los CDC ayuda a los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades a salvar y mejorar vidas desatando el poder de colaboración entre los CDC, organizaciones filantrópicas, empresas, organizaciones y personas para proteger la salud y la seguridad de los Estados Unidos y el mundo. La Fundación de los CDC es la organización sin fines de lucro de confianza autorizada por el Congreso para movilizar socios filantrópicos y recursos del sector privado para respaldar la misión fundamental de los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades de proteger la salud. Desde 1995, la Fundación de los CDC ha recaudado más de $1600 millones de dólares y ha lanzado más de 1200 programas que han causado impacto en una serie de amenazas para la salud, que incluyen desde enfermedades crónicas, como las enfermedades cardiovasculares y el cáncer, hasta enfermedades infecciosas como las causadas por el rotavirus y el VIH, hasta respuestas a emergencias, como las respuestas al COVID-19 y al Ébola. El año pasado, la Fundación de los CDC manejó cientos de programas en los Estados Unidos y en más de 160 países. Puesto que los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades son una agencia federal, todos los descubrimientos científicos que son resultado de investigaciones de los CDC están disponibles para el público y la comunidad científica en general para su revisión. Los fondos proporcionados por la Fundación de los CDC para tareas a realizar por los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades no dependen del resultado de las investigaciones ni de que una actividad científica sea favorable a uno o más socios. La Fundación de los CDC trabaja con los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades para garantizar que los programas tengan un efecto significativo para los CDC y la salud pública, y suplementen las prioridades y el trabajo constante de los CDC. Los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades y la Fundación de los CDC tienen procedimientos de evaluación establecidos para protegerse de posibles conflictos de intereses. Si desea obtener más información, visite la página www.cdcfoundation.org . * Nota * Los enlaces a sitios web pueden llevar a páginas en inglés o español. Última revisión: el 15 de julio del 2022 Fuente: Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades

pages.text: Alaska's Mineral Men | Bureau of Land Management Skip to main navigation Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Alaska's Mineral Men Aug 8, 2025 Gold is king in Alaska. Specifically, placer gold, which comprises the vast majority of mining sites in this mineral-rich state. Regardless of what the mine produces, all mining and mining reclamation sites on land managed by the BLM must be regularly inspected by folks like geologist Fred Transburg and environmental protection specialist Tony Gallagher from the BLM Anchorage Field Office (AFO). But there’s far more to their jobs than inspecting a site; Transburg and Gallagher are part of a team that maintains the productivity of Alaska’s mining industry while preventing unnecessary or undue degradation (UUD) of the land. Part of the reason for the job’s complexity has to do with shared authority. BLM Alaska doesn’t actually issue permits for miners: the State of Alaska does. However, BLM authorizes use of the federal land before permits are issued and regularly monitors the site after the issuance. Both the state and the BLM can shut down operations. Mine inspections ensure mine sites are in compliance with standards set by the current administration and by state and federal agencies. Figure 1: Transburg (right) and environmental protection specialist Justin Burrows (left) document mining activity surface disturbances east of Cantell. Photo by Tony Gallagher (BLM). BLM mine inspectors act as a sort of liaison between the state of Alaska and its miners, ensuring that every miner understands the steps they must follow and the prerequisites they must meet. Inspections are only done after pre-planning coordination is done and a mine and/or mine reclamation plan is approved. From there, inspectors go over everything in the plan to ensure proper techniques are being followed. “It’s a lot of paperwork and a lot of steps that can be hard to understand, which is why we try to help our miners navigate through them,” says Transburg. The state also has its own separate inspections carried out by Alaska DNR mining compliance staff. What’s inspected is based on the site’s unique mining or mining reclamation plan, so inspections vary widely by site. Environmental protection specialists like Gallagher may also conduct soil and water testing at the mine sites. Figure 2: Transburg inspects the fire damage at a historic stamp mill in the McGrath area. Photo by Tony Gallagher (BLM). In accordance with the BLM’s multiple-use mission, the primary reason for BLM inspections is to prevent unnecessary or undue (UUD) degradation of the land. Alaska’s mining compliance team is unique. Transburg explains it’s probably one of the highest-preforming groups in the country due to the remoteness of Alaska’s mines, especially when you take the state’s size and lack of infrastructure into account. Transburg’s favorite parts of the job are collaborating with miners and mining professionals across the state and traveling to help other field offices. Whereas Gallagher’s favorite part is the sense of fulfillment that comes from doing work important to Alaska and its residents. “They [the miners] are good people,” says Gallagher, and fostering relationships with them is beneficial for the state and its mining industry. Inspections are an integral part of BLM mining practices and our multiple-use mission. By acting as a proponent for miners across the state, the BLM is helping to unleash Alaska’s critical minerals. Figure 3: Environmental protection specialist Tony Gallagher unpacks a supply drop for emergency overflow prevention at a site in the McGrath area. Photo by Fred Transburg (BLM). Story by: Jordan Old

pages.title: ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump? | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
pages.description: Circumstances are ripe for change in this onetime Republican stronghold given the current dissatisfaction with Trump agenda, experts say
pages.text: ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump? | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Voters wait in line to cast their ballots at a polling place on 5 November 2024 in Scottsdale, Arizona. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Voters wait in line to cast their ballots at a polling place on 5 November 2024 in Scottsdale, Arizona. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images US midterm elections 2026 ‘A revolution in slow motion’: is Arizona’s wealthiest district finally done with Trump? Circumstances are ripe for change in this onetime Republican stronghold given the current dissatisfaction with Trump agenda, experts say Mary Jo Pitzl in Scottsdale, Arizona Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.33 EDT First published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google D onald Trump has repeatedly asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot in November’s crucial midterm elections. And in the comfortable confines of Arizona’s most affluent and fiercely contested congressional district, Trump is definitely on voters’ minds. But whether that helps or hurts the warring congressional candidates in this sun-drenched swath of suburbia, where Teslas and walled-in luxury homes dominate, depends on who you ask. “Any politician on the face of the Earth who’s a Republican is not getting my vote,” Tom Wolfe, a lifelong Republican, said while sitting down to a lunch of a burger and fries. Trump’s endorsement was a “death knell”, the 82-year-old said. He plans to vote for Democrats in next week’s elections. For David McGahan, a retired accountant reveling in his retirement life in Rio Verde, a desert enclave outside Scottsdale, the economy and the country are working well under Trump. “I like the course the country is on,” McGahan said while pumping gas at a local Costco. “Mostly,” he conceded, when a reporter noted the $101 charge for his fill-up. Cushioned between blue cities and red counties, America’s suburbs have emerged nationally as political battlegrounds. That is especially true of Arizona’s first congressional district, which includes north Scottsdale and Paradise Valley. Here, among the high-end golf courses and desert estates with breathtaking mountain views, the competition between Democrat Amish Shah – an emergency room doctor who narrowly lost the seat in 2024 – and Republican Jay Feely – a former National Football League kicker backed by Trump – could help determine control of the House in November. View image in fullscreen Amish Shah, who is seeking the Democratic nomination for Arizona’s first congressional district, speaks to supporters at a friend’s home on 21 July 2026, in Phoenix. Photograph: Wufei Yu/AP Since Trump’s election a decade ago, Republicans’ hold on the district has slipped, though the party still maintains a voter registration advantage. The seat is open, after the Republican congressman David Schweikert opted to not seek a ninth term. “These are your McCain-type voters,” said Matt Grodsky, a Democratic political strategist referring to the late Arizona senator and 2008 Republican presidential nominee, John McCain. They’re business owners, hold college degrees and relatively tuned in to politics. Given the current dissatisfaction with the Trump agenda and no incumbent with built-in name ID, Grodsky said circumstances were ripe for a change in this onetime Republican stronghold. “If there’s going to be a swing,” he said, “it should be this cycle.” W ith a median income of $102,000, 33% of residents holding a bachelor’s degree and 22% with an advanced degree, voters in the district lean conservative, but don’t fit comfortably in Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement , said Mike Noble, founder of Noble Predictive Insights, a non-partisan pollster based in Arizona. Historic preservation is a conversation with our past about our future. It provides us with opportunities to ask, "What is important in our history?" and "What parts of our past can we preserve for the future?" Through historic preservation, we look at history in different ways, ask different questions of the past, and learn new things about our history and ourselves. pages.text: Median Annual Earnings Map | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Median Annual Earnings Map Median Annual Earnings by State and Disability, 2023 The interactive map below shows 2023 median earnings by state and disability status for workers age 16 or older with any earnings in the year. Earnings include income from wages, salary, self-employment, or a personal business or farm but do not include other sources such as Social Security, pensions, public assistance, rental income, or investment earnings. Hover, tap, or use tab/arrow keys to see earnings data by state. Use the drop-down menu to see earnings by disability status; click on legend items to hide or view states within each earnings band. To see the data in table form or to download in .csv format, use the Options menu. Median earnings Workers with disabilities Workers without disabilities All workers Highlights In every U.S. state, workers with disabilities had lower median earnings than those without disabilities. On average nationwide, workers with disabilities earned 31% less than their nondisabled peers. Other highlights from the 2023 data include: States with the highest median annual earnings for workers with disabilities: District of Columbia, Maryland, Hawaii, Washington, New Jersey, Virginia, and Alaska. States with the lowest median annual earnings for workers with disabilities: Vermont, Mississippi, New Mexico, Montana, Idaho, Michigan, and Iowa. State with the smallest earnings gap: Nevada, where workers with disabilities earned 83% of what their nondisabled peers earned. State with the largest earnings gap: Vermont, where workers with disabilities earned 55% of what workers without disabilities did. These comparisons are unadjusted, meaning that they do not account for differences in hours worked, occupation, education, or other factors that may influence earnings. In addition, these data show broad patterns, not causes, of earnings differences between people with disabilities and those without. Last Updated: July 02, 2025

Process to Determine Whether Areas Meet the NAAQS (Designations Process) Process of Setting and Implementing NAAQS Standards - setting, reviewing, and revising the standards Designations - determining whether areas meet the standards Implementation - attaining and maintaining the standards After EPA sets a new National Ambient Air Quality Standard or revises an existing standard for a criteria air pollutant , the Clean Air Act requires EPA to determine if areas of the country meet the new standards. Within one year of setting a new or revised national ambient air quality standard for a criteria pollutant, States and tribes submit recommendations to the EPA as to whether or not an area is attaining the standard. The states and tribes base these recommendations on available air quality data collected from monitors at locations in urban and rural settings as well as other information characterizing air quality such as modeling. After working with the states and tribes and considering the information from air quality monitors, and/or models, EPA will "designate" an area based on whether or not it is meeting the standard. If the air quality in a geographic area meets or is cleaner than the national standard, it is called an attainment area (designated “attainment/unclassifiable”); areas that don't meet the national standard are called nonattainment areas. In some cases, EPA is not able to determine an area's status after evaluating the available information and those areas are designated "unclassifiable." Once designations take effect, state and local governments with nonattainment areas must develop implementation plans outlining how areas will attain and maintain the standards by reducing air pollutant emissions. Tribes may elect to develop tribal implementation plans but are not required to do so. Adobe Acrobat Reader (PDF) Description: Adobe Acrobat Reader is a program that allows users to view files in Portable Document Format (PDF). PDF is a universal file format that preserves the appearance of the original document. PDF files can be easily printed but not easily modified. Several documents throughout this Web site are available in PDF. These files contain complex documents with graphs, images, and special text that cannot be presented easily through the typical Web browser. The creator of this file format, Adobe® Systems, offers a free viewer so that you can view any PDF file.
